I am only pointing out to him that what he does in that respect is to oblige the submarine commander by reporting for that commander to his base that successful action has been taken. My hon. friend, or anyone else who publishes a statement of this kind, does it-unwittingly of course-for the submarine commander. Mr. Speaker, with much of what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has said, I am in thorough agreement, but I think it would have been better if it had been stated a long time ago, after the first incident, just what was the proper course to pursue. That was not done. I may say to the minister that I heard of this incident myself on Tuesday. Reports were widespread in the province of Quebec, and I have had many letters about it. I communicated with the minister on my arrival from Fredericton at noon on Tuesday; he told me what the position was as they understood it and indicated just the reason the minister has now given-that a substantial time should elapse before the incident should be made public. I am in thorough agreement with that. If that course had been proposed to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy)
I have no doubt that as a good citizen he would have been guided by it. At Matane and Cap Chat the situation was such that everybody knew7 it. From a letter I received only this morning I could tell the minister just how widespread was the information about this incident. You cannot keep these things quiet. However, an announcement in the House of Commons is another matter.
There is one thing I should like the minister to bring to the attention of his colleague. What is the position with respect to convoys in the St. Lawrence? Are there any? Should we not know the position, at least in a general way? The minister shakes his head. Perhaps he is right; I am not going to judge. But so far we do not know just what is the position with respect to protection. I think it would have a reassuring effect if something were said on that point.

maintopic: CONSIDERATIONS AFFECTING ANNOUNCEMENTS AS TO SINKINGS

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Hon. ANGUS L. MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): I should like to make a statement with reference to certain remarks made in this house on Friday last by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy). I might recall to the house that on May 12, I believe it was, I gave a statement to the press, and on the 13th I made a statement in this house, respecting sinkings on the eastern Canadian coast. In those statements I endeavoured' to lay down certain rules which should guide in further pronouncements of this nature. Subsequently to those dates, the chief censor for Canada, Colonel Biggar, in cooperation with the officers of the naval services, issued a circular which was directed to the newspapers of the country setting forth in greater detail the considerations which

should be kept in mind in making statements of this sort. I am very glad to say that the newspapers of this country have observed with the greatest care the suggestions made to them by Colonel Biggar.
I should like to point out that in Great Britain announcements of sinkings of merchant ships are not now made. For a time in the earlier days of the war it was the custom, in due course, to announce that certain vessels had been sunk and that the next of kin of the casualties, if there were any, had been notified. But in more recent months you will not find any such reports of sinkings in the British press. There are excellent reasons for that. In the first place any immediate announcement of sinkings will prevent the next of kin of casualties from being informed before the announcement is made. The result is that every person who has a friend or relative on these ships sailing the seas is in anxiety until he gets a letter from that friend. Consequently it is only proper, in common decency and Christianity, to wait for some time, and to inform the next of kin of casualties, and when the announcement of the sinking is made, to say that that has been done. Then everyone who has not been notified knows that his relative or friend is not involved in the sinking.
There is another reason, the main reason of course, which is that announcements of this sort are likely to give useful information to the enemy. That is the chief reason why some secrecy has to be maintained. The ways in which announcements of this sort may be of use to the enemy are many and varied. If he does not get the information from us, he has to work it out for himself. He has to separate rumour from fact; he has to judge of the reliability of his information, and in a hundred ways he may remain uncertain. But when we in this country, and particularly in this house, give him the information on a platter, then the thing is settled and he does not need to inquire any further as to the accuracy of the information.
As I say, the hon. member for Gaspe last Friday did not ask a question but made a statement. He said that three ships out of a convoy of fourteen had been sunk. The hon. member having made that statement, and having made it, I must assume, with every sense of his responsibility as a member of this house, and the matter having therefore become public and having been announced in the press of the country and on the radio of the country, I may now state, I think I am almost required to state to the house, that three ships belonging to the united nations were torpedoed and sunk in the gulf of St. Law-

Slapping Losses
rence about a week ago. I must add with regret that four members of the crews of those ships are known to have been killed, four are reported missing, and ninety-nine have been safely landed. I am glad to say one pleasant thing in what must be an unpleasant duty, and that is that the citizens of that region, the constituents of my hon. friend, and of other hon. members of this house too perhaps, have shown in this and in the other instance which occurred two months ago, the highest measure of charity and kindliness. They are not, I understand, wealthy people, they have little to give, but what they had to give they gave with a cheerful heart to those men who were perhaps worse off than themselves.
Information as to the sinking of these ships was in the possession of many people early last week. There is no doubt about that. Many people knew of it; it was known along the waterfronts of the country, it was known to the press by Monday or Tuesday of last week. The press refused to publish it; not one newspaper, so far as I know, endeavoured to make any use of this information until an official statement was made. It was in the possession of mjr hon, friend the leader of the opposition, because he had heard the story on the train and spoke to me about it. I felt it quite proper to inform my hon. friend as to the facts, asking him-what perhaps I did not have to ask him, because I knew I could rely on his good sense in the matter-to say nothing about it, and of course my hon. friend said nothing about it. So the information was widely known to people in this country. But I point out now-and it is a mistake that is commonly made-that people say to me, "Well, the public know about this anyway; why don't you make an announcement about it?" But there is a tremendous difference between Canadians knowing about something and Germans knowing about it. The entire people of this country might know of a sinking or some other event of that kind, but so long as that information did not get to Germany, so long as it was not made public in our papers or broadcast over our radio, the chances of its getting to Germany would be small. Of course once it is broadcast it becomes the property of the world. It is known in the United States, it becomes known in neutral countries; speedily it finds its way to Germany and is used there for propaganda purposes.
These rules laid down two months ago and repeated by the chief censor are not made for the purpose of keeping information from the people of Canada-not at all. They are made for the sole purpose of keeping
from the enemy information which may be of great value to him in directing the movement of his ships.
This brings up a much more serious question, one which concerns the rights and privileges of this house. There is very little use, there is very little purpose, in censoring the press and radio of the country if any hon. member of this house can stand in his place and, by asking a question, or by making a direct statement, as the hon. member for Gaspe did, undo the whole work of the censorship authorities and all the efforts of those who are endeavouring to ensure the safety of allied ships and allied seamen. We are constantly urging the average citizen to guard ihis	tongue. You see	noticesin almost	every	elevator. in public
buildings, in government buildings, urging people not to talk about the movements of ships or troops or the manufacture of munitions. "Guard your tongues", we are telling the people in French and English all the time. But how can we expect the average citizen of this country to guard his tongue if hon. members of this house do not guard theirs?
I will say this to the hon. member for Gaspe; had I been in the house on Friday I think I should have felt constrained to rise and ask this house to expunge from the record the statement which he made. Thereby it would not have become a public statement. But he having made it, and it having been allowed to stand on Hansard, it of course became public; and the members of the press gallery had a right to use it. But if this sort of thing is to go on; if any hon. member can stand up and, by innuendo, by question, by statement, jeopardize the whole security system of this country, then I am afraid it will be necessaiy for someone to say that statements of that kind will either not be allowed to be made or, if made, will not become part of the record of this house.
My hon. friend talks of the protection of his constituents. I would say to my hon. friend that statements such as he made are not adding a single jot or tittle to the safety of his constituents; on the contrary they endanger the lives of his constituents. I would say further that there are other people in this country, other citizens of Canada, who are in greater danger, or are much nearer the battle line, much nearer the danger zone, than his constituents; and not once have I heard from that easternmost part of Canada any break of this kind. Not once have I heard an hon. member from the easternmost provinces of Canada rise in his place and ask questions of this kind. Not once in the newspapers of that part of the country, where information as to the movements of ships is fuller and more complete than anywhere elsp.
Shipping Losses

have I heard of anyone endeavouring to say anything or to do anything which might endanger the life of a single seaman or the safety of a single ship. When my hon. friend talks about protecting his constituents, I should like to know what he has ever done to ensure the greater protection of this country, or to add in any way to its defences.

maintopic: CONSIDERATIONS AFFECTING ANNOUNCEMENTS AS TO SINKINGS
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CONSIDERATIONS AFFECTING ANNOUNCEMENTS AS TO SINKINGS
speechtext: Placing the whole burden upon an hon. member of this house to ask about something that occurs in his constituency, and then castigating him, in my opinion is wrong. The minister must take ' some responsibility for this situation. As for the radio and the press, surely we have a voluntary censorship; and members of the house surely must ask questions somewhere about the welfare of their constituents or as to what happens in their constituencies.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: CONSIDERATIONS AFFECTING ANNOUNCEMENTS AS TO SINKINGS
speechtext: I realize that we should not get into a debate, Mr. Speaker, but my hon. friend could have asked his question privately if he had wished, as my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) did. Then he would have been given the information on his honour as a member of the house. But I do not understand how the asking of a question or the making of a statement in this house is going to add to the protection of my hon. friend's constituents. If he thinks for one moment that the whole Canadian navy is going to line up along his shores and defend those shores only, letting the convoy system we have and the protection we have for all the rest of Canada go to the dogs, he is making a tremendous mistake. I am not ready to change the disposition of one ship of the Canadian navy for him or all the questions he may ask from now until doomsday.

maintopic: CONSIDERATIONS AFFECTING ANNOUNCEMENTS AS TO SINKINGS
speechtext:
I have listened to the minister very carefully, and I am taking his remarks in the best spirit, because I know the motives which inspire him are of the best. He has asked me what I have ever done to protect my constituents and my constituency. I would recall that I have offered the government many suggestions which have been disregarded; and if they had listened to what I suggested, this last torpedoing might not have happened.
I will not disclose anything now. My reason for making that announcement-which I will admit might not have been as good as I 
thought it was-was in support of my asking for a secret session for the benefit of the house. I have the strongest reasons for urging a secret session, in order to disclose to parliament matters I do not want to disclose publicly, because I am afraid they would help the enemy. That was the only reason for my announcement. If we are given a secret session to study these important matters I will prove to the house that I am just as good and loyal a Canadian, taking just as good care of my constituency and of the interests of the whole country, as anyone else.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: CONSIDERATIONS AFFECTING ANNOUNCEMENTS AS TO SINKINGS
speechtext: If I may add one word, if my hon. friend has in mind any means for adding to the protection of this country I should be very glad if he would come and tell me so. We do not need a secret session so far as naval defences are concerned. If the hon. member will come to me at any time with his suggestions I shall be glad to entertain them.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SHORTAGE OF FARM HELP
subsubtopic: CONTROL OF AGRICUL- TURAL WAGES-HARVEST LEAVE FOR MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: Can the Minister of Agriculture make a statement to the house so that the people of western Canada, and particularly the farmers, may know what steps are being taken to meet the very serious situation regarding farm and harvest labour? I am moved to make this inquiry because of the number of letters I am receiving which indicate that the farmers are seriously worried about the matter. What cooperation is being given by the various war services? What is being done?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: SHORTAGE OF FARM HELP
subsubtopic: CONTROL OF AGRICUL- TURAL WAGES-HARVEST LEAVE FOR MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
The question should really be
directed to the Minister of Labour, who handles all questions which have to do with labour, including even labour for farms. I may say that representations are made to me as Minister of Agriculture, as apparently they are made to various hon. members representing agricultural constituencies, and I make representations on behalf of those concerned to the Department of Labour. My understanding is-the Minister of Labour will correct me if I am wrong-that a vote of $100,000 has been set up by this house for the purpose of making it possible for the minister to assist the provincial governments, or whatever department of a provincial government deals with agricultural labour matters, in the organization and transportation of labour from one part of a province to another, or even, if necessary, from one .province to another. For two or three years an amount of money has been included in the estimates for that purpose, and agreements are reached between the Minister of Labour, together with his department, and whatever department is responsible in the province, under which assistance will be given for the organization and transportation of whatever surplus labour is available to be moved to areas where there is a shortage.
Speaking as Minister of Agriculture, though, I think I should say-what is probably known to all hon. members-that surplus labour for different purposes is becoming less and less. Practically all of the labour in Canada is now employed, either in the armed services, in manufacturing, in transportation, or on farms, and I believe it to be very difficult to muster any additional amount of labour for farming purposes. It might be possible to reorganize it and to shift some of the surplus labour which is not on farms from place to place in
Labour Conditions

order 'to have it better distributed, but I doubt if there is any considerable amount of additional labour which can be placed on the farms. The course I have mentioned has been urged on the Department of Labour and they are doing, I believe, everything possible to coordinate the efforts of the provinces and the federal authority in this direction. An attempt is being made to - organize all the surplus urban labour, in villages and towns in the different provinces, in order that they can go to the farms in the surrounding community for so many hours a day or so many days a week. Organization is proposed similar to the organization which was carried- on in the last two years of the last war.
So far as the defence services are concerned, I think the Minister of National Defence should speak on their behalf.

subtopic: SHORTAGE OF FARM HELP
subsubtopic: CONTROL OF AGRICUL- TURAL WAGES-HARVEST LEAVE FOR MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext: In further reference to the question which the Minister of Agriculture has just been answering, may I direct a question in respect to farm labour to the Minister of Labour, who seems to be the proper authority? It is becoming increasingly difficult, as the Minister of Agriculture said, to get suitable farm labour; and we are faced with this situation, that although we are paying double the wages we paid a few years ago, certain people will try to outbid us and steal away our help. I have had a recent illustration of this on my own farm. I should like to ask the minister if the same regulations should not apply to farm labour as apply to labour in factories-that the permission of the employer must be obtained before a man leaves to take another job of a similar character.

subtopic: SHORTAGE OF FARM HELP
subsubtopic: CONTROL OF AGRICUL- TURAL WAGES-HARVEST LEAVE FOR MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
I would say, in a kindly way, that we have heard a great deal about an allout war effort, and it is rather good1, from the labour man's point of view, to hear that there is a shortage of labour in Ontario.
As long ago as last February the Minister of Agriculture and myself discussed this matter, anticipating a distinct shortage of labour on the farms of this country. We came to an arrangement with the government of Ontario, who last year, through the instrumentality of an agreement with the federal government, and in cooperation with the employment service of Canada, made possible the organization of 23,000 additional people for the farms of that province. We made a similar agreement this year, with an additional amount beyond that of last year of $40,000 apiece, making $200,000 for the two governments. We sent a copy of that agreement to

all the other provinces, as we thought they would like to avail themselves of similar provisions or similar facilities.
I think this may be fairly stated1, that in connection with agriculture generally the best kind of government organization is that which is closest to the people.. I do not say that in any way to get from under the responsibility of the federal government. There is no need to tell my hon. friend that in its very essence agriculture changes from province to province, so that the problem in Saskatchewan is different from the problem in Ontario. Both in industry and in agriculture, faced as we are with various problems, we think it will be necessary to take substitutes. It is hard for us to adjust ourselves to a condition that departs from the psychology of two or three years ago, when we could simply go to the shelf and take down what we wanted. We have reached the point where it will be necessary for farmers and industrialists in Canada to use, if I may say so, all their local powers, their energy and their imagination to meet the local situation.
With respect to the wages question raised by my hon. friend, I should like to go into that, but he knows as well as I do, that in all these matters agriculture is generally excepted. It is excepted from the provisions of the unemployment insurance act; it is excepted from the provisions of many other acts and regulations in force in Canada, and I should not like to give an answer offhand. The hon. member understands as well as I do the vast organization that would be necessary to enable us to exercise control over the wages of individual farm labourers throughout the country. With regard to industry, it is comparatively easy where there are big units, where the organization is complete and we know who the employers are. There are 150,000 employers in industry and commerce to-day each of whom employs more than fifteen people. I say that not to make a speech, but to point out to my hon. friend the difficulties with which the government would be confronted if it undertook to set in motion immediately a policy that would control agricultural wages.
I think we should stand by the good old British principle, that it is wise not to pass regulations and orders in council unless there is a reasonable chance of enforcing them, because lack of enforcement would bring the government into ill repute and also render difficult the application and stabilization of the wage structure ot commerce and industry in this country.

I wish I were justified in giving to my hon. friend, the house and the country, an assurance that consideration which would really result favourably could be given. But all cases will have to be considered individually, and there will be no harvest leave in the broad sense of making a general order that such leave will be granted to men who are needed to work on farms. Some consideration may be given regarding personnel in some units of a special character such as I have indicated, but I am afraid I cannot give the house any further assurance than that. '

speechtext:
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved the third reading of Bill No. 64, to assist in the carrying on and coordination of vocational training (title changed to "An Act respecting the Carrying on and Coordination of Vocational Training.")
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Fournier (Hull) in the chair.
Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the schedule to the Excise Act, 1934, and to provide:-
1. That the duty of excise on spirits distilled in Canada be increased from seven dollars to nine dollars per proof gallon, provided that duty paid spirits owned by any distiller at the close of business on the twenty-third day of June, one thousand nine hundred and forty-two shall be subject to the following additional duty of excise on every gallon of the strength of proof two dollars and so in proportion for any greater or less strength than the strength of proof and for any less quantity than a gallon.

It will be recalled that in my speech on the budget on June 30 last I adverted to the question of increased excise and import duties on alcoholic beverages. I do not intend to-day to repeat the observations I made then. I am fearful of the tremendous increase in the drink bill of this country at a time when Canada is at war, and I think something ought to be done about it. On one or two occasions when this matter has been referred to in the house the minister has taken the ground-I suppose it is open to him to take it-that in Canada the retail sale of liquor is entirely in the hands of the provincial governments. It is true that we have a system of government control of liquor in every province, save one, Prince Edward Island, where they go through the form of having a prohibitory law on their statute book. In my view this is not government control at all; it is government monopoly. We have had the spectacle, at all events in my province, and I am bound to say before the war, of the authorities actually doing certain things to promote the sale of liquor. I have always deprecated this, because I felt it was wrong.
Excise Act Amendment

I am not approaching this subject matter from the point of view of ethics. I am not advocating prohibition, I do not think prohibition can succeed in this country without the overwhelming support of the public. That is not apparent now, and it was not apparent for many years while prohibition was on the statute books of certain of the provinces. I am approaching the matter purely and simply from the point of view of a nation at war, a nation straining every effort it can to raise money for the prosecution of the war. I hope the minister will reconsider his position with respect to this matter. It is obvious that this is purely a revenue measure. If the minister is candid, and I am sure he will be, he will affirm that position. In so far as it is a revenue measure I am sure it will be supported, because if there is one thing upon which taxes should be imposed, both in war time and in peace time, it is on intoxicating liquors. For the moment I am differentiating between spirits as such, and beer and other lighter commodities.
We have the spectacle of the gross sales of liquor in Canada, under government monopoly, mounting to almost phenomenal proportions, and the thoughtful people and .good citizens of this country are alarmed about that situation. In my own province, in the year 1935, the total profits from the sale *of liquor at government liquor stores was between $500,000 and $600,000. In the fiscal year ended October 31. 1941, the profits were four times as much, and to-day, with the great decrease in the sale of gasoline and a large number of cars not being licensed, I suppose the liquor monopoly now in the hands of the provinces is the largest single source of revenue they have, or many of them at all events. As time goes on they come to look upon that as a legitimate source of revenue. It is legal, it is very easy money, and so it is quite natural for them to do so. I have never myself felt it to be a high type of citizenship to desire to be relieved of my obligations as a citizen to pay revenue to the province at the expense, perhaps of my weaker brother. But to-day I am not taking that high exalted stand. I am trying to deal with the matter in the light of present developments. Should we not do something to cut down this huge bill and divert to better purposes some of this free money that is now devoted to liquor? I use the word "better"; theoretically perhaps the war is not a better purpose, but at least it is much more of an absolute necessity. It is true that we need this money, and the nine million dollars that we will get from it will mean something to our exchequer, but I think we would get far more effort if some of it were diverted by
[Mr. R. B. Hanson.1
other forms of taxation to the public treasury. I think that would be better than putting excise and import duties on alcoholic beverages.
I have no doubt the minister has it in mind that to restrict the sales and make it much harder for people to get liquor than it now is would revive the old and discreditable corn-ditions with respect to bootlegging. But I might remind him that some of the incentives to bootlegging have been removed by changed circumstances. A great deal of liquor came into my province a few years ago because of its proximity to the two islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, which were a source of supply. But then the United States had prohibition, and rum-running was rampant. I do not know that anybody got very much out of it, but some people are reputed to have made money out of it. The chief outlet was, of course, in the United States. As to central Canada, I have heard various stories about what happened along the border. But now that the United States definitely has liquor, the incentive to smuggling liquor into the United States is no longer there.
This law would not affect that.

It does
not affect anj'thing except the raising of additional revenue. I am trying to deal with a wider principle than that. I am trying to disabuse the minister's mind of any mistaken idea he may have with respect to the return of bootlegging.

I
agree with the hon. member there.

I am trying to talk sense, and I should think my good friend the hon. member for Brantford City would agree with me when I talk sense, which is 100 per cent of the time, I hope. I do submit that we, as representative men of this nation, should give consideration to what after all everybody knows is an evil thing in our body politic-the expenditure in war time of some $250,000,000 for the purchase of alcoholic beverages. I realize that a very large portion of that sum goes into the public treasury. If hon. members were to ascertain the exact figure they would find that a very large portion of that sum goes in taxes to the federal and provincial governments, and that the consumer is paying a good deal for very little in actual commercial value.
We have not rationed liquor. We apply the principle of rationing on the theory of scarcity; that, I think, is the economic reason for rationing. I was very much amused when on the other side last year to be told that

Excise Act Amendment
in a great hotel in Edinburgh they were rationed to four bottles of whisky a day, while down in London you could buy all you could pay for. I could not understand it, because Edinburgh was, I was going to say, the centre of the industry.
That four bottles was for the hotel, not for the individual.

Yes, for the whole hotel to sell to its guests.
It does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that some solution should be found whereby a part of this enormous drink bill would be diverted to a better purpose and used in the war effort. I wonder whether the minister has not given further consideration to that. I am sure that with his background the minister must be alarmed at the situation which has presented itself, say, in Nova Scotia. I have had multitudes of letters from people in Nova Scotia complaining of the huge amount of money which has been diverted from the armed forces, we will say, to the purchase and consumption of liquor. I do hope that some consideration will be given to mitigating, I am not going to say the evil, but the amount of the bill which this nation has to pay. And that can be done.
I have no suggestion to make other than that of pressure, or that some arrangement be made with the provincial governments to limit the sale of liquor; because I agree that a large part of the problem is on the doorstep of the provincial governments, and not particularly on the minister's. I noticed in the press the other day that the government in Newfoundland has had to deal with this problem. I did not think their efforts were very stringent, because I understand that a man there can still buy three bottles of whisky a week, and surely that ought to be enough for anybody. But I do submit that the minister should make some effort in conjunction with the provincial governments., as a war measure, to limit the sale of liquor in Canada in order that a large portion of this bill of $250,000,000 may be diverted into other and better channels. I suggest that the minister negotiate with the provincial governments. I think some of them have been seriously alarmed at the situation that has developed in certain of the provinces. I think in the province of Nova Scotia they have taken note of public opinion and they themselves have gone so far, perhaps not very far, in an effort to decrease the sale of liquor. I do not think very much has been done in my ou-n province.
This resolution is purely a revenue measure. I do not disagree with that from the point of
view of getting money for the war, but I believe that if we were to use other methods a much larger portion of this spirits bill could be diverted to war purposes without any detriment to the liberty of any subject, and with great benefit to the whole body politic.

I completely agree with the remarks of the leader of the opposition. At a time when the very necessities of life are being restricted, I cannot understand why this country should tolerate the expenditure of $250,000,000 a year on liquor. I would especially call the attention of the authorities to the facilities which are reported to be available to soldiers to enable them lo procure hard liquor. I do not see how you can train an army on liquor. I agree that the men should be allowed to get beer if they need it, but it is appalling the way money is spent, especially in my city, on strong liquor. It is of no use to those who consume it, or to their families, and it occasions scandal at a time when people are asked to make the sacrifices they are now called upon to make.
It is all very well to say that a large part of this expenditure is returned to the government in taxes. I recall seeing recently the financial statement of a company which shows that, while they are paying $11,000,000 to the federal treasury, they still have at their disposal $10,000,000 to pay to the shareholders.

I think
the government would take a good deal of that.

That is irrespective of the tremendous amount of money which is expended on advertisements and propaganda of various kinds.
I suggest that careful consideration be given to the remarks of the leader of the opposition, with a view to having this tax increased to the highest possible percentage. As I recall it, in the last war federal and provincial taxes combined amounted to $17 a gallon. At that time opposition was expressed to the impost because it was said that it encouraged bootlegging. But since those days, nearly thirty years ago, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have organized a most efficient system to discover bootlegging; there is no more of this menace in the country, and I think something could very well be done to put liquor on practically a prohibitory basis. It is not a necessity of life, although it may be needed in certain types of sickness or other extraordinary cases. In a general way hard liquor is one of the luxuries, and if a man wants to have a drink he should be required to pay for it. At a time when we are cutting
Excise Act Amendment

expenses and asking people to make sacrifices, to take less sugar and tea, to buy fewer suits or shirts, even to the point of depriving their families of things they need, in order to win the war, why should they be confronted with a figure such as $250,000,000, advertising these scandalous conditions in the midst of the war? I wholly agree with the remarks of the leader of the opposition.

I agree in large measure with what the leader of the opposition has said. No doubt far too much drinking of alcoholic liquors is going on at this time, and too great a part of our effort is diverted to the manufacture of them. How this can be avoided, however, it is difficult for me to understand. I do not believe any of us would want to go back to the days of prohibition. The hon. member for [DOT]Quebec West and South, who immediately preceded me, suggested that we should again have prohibition or should put liquor practically on a prohibitory basis. It is my conviction that the Ontario Temperance Act, which was in effect in Ontario about a decade ago, did more to bring about intemperance and excessive drinking than any measure which was ever placed on the statute book of that province. Hon. members from Ontario will remember that although there was supposed to be prohibition, in almost every centre were numerous places where people could obtain liquor illicitly; also numbers of persons persisted in carrying around liquor in their pockets. Prior to that time, when I was a young man, I would never think of going to a dance with liquor on me; none of the young men of my day would have done so. But when the Ontario Temperance Act came into effect, I noticed that practically all the young men, and, I am sorry to say, many young women, carried liquor with them. We do not want that condition to arise again in Ontario or any part of Canada.
I believe we are all in accord with the curtailment of the sale of intoxicating liquors if it is possible to do so, but I would remind the Minister of Finance that it is not going to be an easy matter. He may increase the tax, he may cut down the sales, but if at the *same time bootleggers flourish and the illicit sale of liquor continues or increases, his efforts will be of no avail. No doubt something should be done, but let us not act without giving the matter most careful consideration, to make sure that we do not have another era of illicit liquor-selling in this country.

I have not said much on this question, but I have thought a good deal. There is no use in trying to bring in legisla-[.Mr. Parent.]
tion unless public support is behind it. I think it is well understood that the minister has the backing of the best men and women in Canada in support of his legislation.
What legislation?

My only criticism is that the tax on hard liquor is not high enough. You cannot make men sober by legislation. I have had a good deal of experience in trying to sober up men when they had gone the limit. You have a better chance of sobering men with strong coffee than you have with legislation against the liquor business. A change of heart is needed. I have no patience with those who think that the dominion and provincial governments can legislate the liquor business out of existence; they cannot do it. I should like to know whether this legislation is in any way related to the discovery of an illicit still in the province of Quebec. It is evident the police are on the job and are going to back up the minister's policy.

The reason which appeals
to me as the ground for the increase in the sale of liquor in the country is the fact that the income of the Canadian people has increased so tremendously. It does appear to me that the mere putting on of 50 or 60 cents for an imperial quart of some kind of liquor will not in itself have the effect of prohibiting the sale of that liquor. I presume the reason the minister has put this tax on is that he sees in it another fairly easy way of increasing the revenues of the country, and also of cutting down generally the purchasing power that is available for other consumer goods. When the statement is made that there is too great a diversion of man-power and materials towards the production of liquor and away from the war effort, the minister might put figures on Hansard, if they are available, as to the total amount spent in Canada on liquor of all kinds, and the total amount of taxes obtained by the dominion government last year-he has given an indication as to what the increase in revenues will be-so that we can arrive at the net amount that is being paid to the producers of these commodities, and thus interpret the amount of labour that is being used and possibly obtain some understanding of the quantity of materials used, and so on.

I suggest that there should also be something in the way of a time limit.
I am well aware of the anxiety of the minister to do his best, but I am aware also
that the people of Ontario are heartily sick of this business. I do not agiee with those

Excise Act Amendment
who have said that drinking was worse during prohibition. I spend a good deal of my time among the rougher element, and I have seen more drunks recently than I did in prohibition days. One hon. gentleman suggested that something should be done, but ended up by saying that nothing should be done. We have reached the stage now where action should be taken. We have come to the pass where there should be some curtailment in time, and the matter should be talked over with the provincial governments. Surely we do not think that the ladies' beer parlours are something that we should be proud of. How would any hon. member like to see his daughter or sister coming out of a ladies' beer parlour, swinging along? Spend some of your time there some time, as I do occasionally. I often drop in on my way home from this house, and I see entertaining times there. I read character in faces, and while there are some Scotch among them, they are not all Scotch. Beer has a more degrading element in it than real whisky. If you want to know that, consider the different races that swing to beer and those that swing to whisky.

"Swing"
is a technical term now, isn't it?

What the aviator drinks after ten o'clock is so many headaches; what he drinks before that may be a little entertainment and amusement. Let him drink his beer as he likes until ten o'clock, but when men reach the headache stage they should quit, so that they can get up next morning with a clear head. When you come to the headache stage, then I think there should be a time limit. The Prime Minister is noted as a splendid man for timing; even in elections he does well, and he would know the time. I do not know whether his experience in liquor is as good as yours and mine, but I suggest that there should be a time limit when men should stop drinking at night if they do not want a headache next morning.
I am a coroner, and I have had to deal with a good many accidents on the road. Often when a man is killed in the county of Wellington and I am called in as coroner, I have had to do some desperate lying-my hon. friend does not have to do that because he is a lawyer. I have sent home word to many a father that a boy had died from heart failure when I knew it was booze. It was the next thing to a sworn declaration, and I made a notorious liar of myself. I am not giving a temperance lecture, but I do suggest that there should be consultation with the provincial governments, because they are charged
with the responsibility of regulating the traffic. There should be some regulation, some curtailment in time, especially among the aviators, and I would be delighted to see the ladies' beer parlours closed. It would be a good thing to see them done away with.

When the war appropriation bill was before the house I spoke at length on this important national question. The large number of letters I have received would indicate that this is a subject that is causing a good deal of anxiety in the homes of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member give me the date of that speech?

June 1. The comments made by hon. members this afternoon also show that this is a subject that should receive more consideration from the government than it has received so far. After speaking on June 1, I received some criticism from certain quarters for suggesting that we should not send beer to the troops in Libya and other battle fronts. I never made such a suggestion. I would not for a moment suggest that those on the battle fronts should be denied the right to have refreshments at their bases. But I do think it is unfortunate that the policy of sending liquid refreshments should be decided by a man who is engaged in the brewing business, and that large quantities are sent when space is needed for more essential material.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not correct. The hon. member is referring to Mr. E. P. Taylor.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, he had nothing to say about that, so far as I know. This beer for Africa was purchased by an agency of the British government and taken by the British government. The only thing the Canadian government could have done would have been to protest, and we did not think we were justified in doing that.
I want to give the government clearance on that. I investigated the matter carefully, and I am prepared to give this government a certificate of non-complicity, if that is a good word.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Thank you.

The information I had was that Mr. Taylor is vice-chairman of this allied shipping council, and he decides how the space shall be used, whether for Bren guns or tanks or beer. The decision was that it should be used for beer, and I was informed that large quantities did move to Libya.
Excise Act Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be so; I do not know. I was simply speaking on behalf of the Canadian government. I do not know what agents of the United Kingdom government acted in the matter. Certainly Mr. Taylor did not take any steps as agent of the Canadian government.
Mr. Taylor in Washington, as vice-chairman of the council, has the responsibility of deciding how the space will be used. He is there as our representative.
No, he is there for the British government.
But he is one of our dollar-a-year men, isn't he?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: .He is an employee of the British government, I believe.
His name was one of those tabled as dollar-a-year men, I remember.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My understanding is that after the late Arthur Purvis died, the British government had to make other arrangements. I do not know the exact position Mr. Taylor occupies, but Mr. Morris Wilson and Mr. Taylor, I believe, or one of them, took on the work that Mr. Purvis had been doing.
Mr. Wilson.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have always regarded Mr. Taylor since that time as a representative, or employee of the United Kingdom government.

The statement placed on record was that:
Mr. E. P. Taylor is one of our dollar-a-year men. . . . Here we have a picture of the British supply council; we see Sir Arthur Salter, Mr. Morris Wilson, Lord Beaverbrook, Mr. E. P. Taylor and Mr. Jean Monnet. The article states that in some respect the British supply council acts as a coordinating body for the allies as well as for the British empire. Listen to this:
"Whether it is an apple or a flying fortress, the British supply organization endeavours to get these goods to the places most in need of assistance."
I think the government of Canada must take responsibility for the decisions made by this council, with Mr. Taylor as one of the members.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have nothing to do with it.

Again I say it is unfortunate that the president of Canadian Breweries should be placed in the position where large quantities of beer manufactured by his company should be going to Libya at a time when it has been established that there was a considerable shortage of other materials of war that are much more effective than beer in

meeting Rommel and the Germans. I support the leader of the opposition in urging that the government give more consideration than has been given to this question.
I hope the minister will answer the question asked by the hon. member for Saskatoon and give some information as to the quantity of materials used in connection with the liquor traffic, and the number of men and women engaged in it. When I spoke on June 1, I mentioned that it was a serious reflection on the people of Saskatchewan that they spent more on liquor last year than the Minister of Finance asked them to raise for the victory loan. It is hardly fair to expect the government of Saskatchewan, hard pressed as it is for funds, to take the lead in seeking to discourage the manufacture and consumption of alcoholic liquors, unless it is part of a national plan. You cannot expect any one province to go out and cut off its revenues unless all parts of the dominion are doing it. I think all hon. members-at least a great many-feel very strongly about this. I would take exception to a statement made by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg some time ago when he suggested that members of this house-
That was in a previous debate.

Yes, but he referred to hon. members of this house. He cast a reflection on this chamber, and the impression has gone out that there is a great deal of drinking by members of this chamber. Let me say that one of the pleasant surprises I have had was to find that a large number of members of this house are total abstainers, and that so little drinking is done by members of the house generally. The reports I heard before coming here were such that I expected there would be more drinking by hon. members, but whatever the shortcomings of this chamber may be, I think the amount of liquor consumed by hon. members is not one of them.
I hope the government will give consideration to the many representations made by temperance and church organizations across the country, and people who are not prohibitionists, to the effect that this be recognized as a national question.
Before this section passes would the minister give some statement regarding the rate of excise in New Zealand, Australia and Great Britain? We are increasing our duty from $7 to $9 a proof gallon; what are the rates in some of these other countries?

I wish to add my voice in support of those who advocate that we curtail the sale of liquor at this time. It has

Excise Act Amendment
been suggested that this is largely a provincial matter, but we have full power to deal with it under the War Measures Act. We have not hesitated to curtail the sale of gasoline and tires and sugar, and there is no reason why we cannot do the same so far as liquor is concerned.
As regards loss of revenue, I do not think anyone would suggest that we should encourage the consumption of a commodity that is injurious to the public, just in order to get revenue from the sale. We might as well encourage the sale of narcotics in order to get revenue.
So far as the tax curtailing the .sale of liquor is concerned, the minister has himself said that the purpose of taxation is to curtail spending; nevertheless I think he realizes that the on!jr real way to stop the sale of any commodity is to ration it. We are finding that out in regard to tires and sugar. I do not believe this country can make a total war effort so long as we allow over-indulgence in the consumption of liquor to prevail as it does to-day.
The liquor industry is consuming a tremendous amount of gasoline and sugar, and is very heavy on tires. As to the stand taken by some hon. members that it is not desirable to go back to the days of prohibition, I am not satisfied at all that if the police really tried to enforce prohibition it could not be enforced. I am not a teetotaller, by any means, but I think we all know that in prohibition days speakeasies and bootlegging were winked at deliberately by the police in many parts of the country. I am satisfied that if any serious attempt were made to enforce prohibition, it could be enforced. But I am not advocating prohibition; I am merely advocating that we ration the sale of liquor. It is a deplorable state of affairs, in a country that is trying to make a total war effort, to see the number of men and women that one can see in a state of intoxication almost any night in any city of this country; and apparently the same thing is going on in England. This tax will not prevent that. It may provide additional revenue, and I am sure the minister would be the last to suggest that he would be willing to sacrifice the health and efficiency of the people in order to get the few dollars that this tax brings in. The only way to curtail the sale is by rationing, not by increasing the tax.

Instead of the various
speakers dealing with this question from the point of view of a tax, we have had several temperance lectures this afternoon. If we want to debate the question of temperance, it is the privilege of any hon. member to bring 44561-262
in a resolution on that question. But the budget is not brought down with the idea of curtailing or rationing liquor, or legislating as to the morals of the people. This budget is for the purpose of raising the necessary money to carry on the war and1 the business of the country. It would perhaps give the people an entirely different picture of this $250,000,000 that is supposed to be spent on alcoholic beverages if the minister would give us not only the correct figures as to the sale, but the tax that is collected by the dominion and the various provinces, the amount of labour, what goes into labour in the form of wages, what goes back to the farmer for his wheat and barley and other grains, and other factors that enter into the manufacture and sale of alcoholic beverages. It might give us a completely different idea of just what this so-called tremendous liquor bill is.
There is one thing about which the minister must be very careful. If we are going to curb this industry, if we are going to bring in special legislation to stop the sale or manufacture, that is an entirely different thing. I am quite in favour of this or any other tax the minister wants to levy, provided that in levying that tax he does not raise the price so high that once more we will see alcohol come in in large quantities from the United States, as happened in former years, when millions of gallons were rushed across. As a matter of fact it is only about two years ago that some very severe sentences were handed out in this connection, so that even under the present tax alcohol has been brought into Canada. That is one thing the minister must watch-that the tax does not make the price too high; for if it does, bootlegging and rum-running will commence immediately, and instead of going from Canada to the United States it will come from the United States to Canada. The matter of prohibition or temperance in itself is a question entirely apart from this matter of raising revenue with which to carry on the business of the country.

I must say that I do not entirely agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. The matter has gone much deeper with the Canadian people than the question of taxation. I think there is a widespread feeling that it is the responsibility of the dominion government to do something about liquor, and not to wash its hands and say this is entirely a problem for the provincial governments. It does seem to me that the minister might give the committee the figures as to expenditures for liquor, both hard and soft, the number of men employed in the

Excise Act Amendment

industry, and the materials used, so that we may have before us the facts on which to form an opinion. I was very much impressed by a full page advertisement which appeared in the Evening Citizen of June 30, published by the Canadian Temperance Federation. According to this advertisement the cost to ultimate consumers of liquor legally sold in Canada has been as follows:
1938		 $173,000,000
1939		 179.000,000
1940	 191.000,000
1941	 232,000,000
The estimate they give for 1942 is $290,000,000. In this advertisement three suggestions are offered, to which I think the minister should give his reaction. They are:
(1)	As the manufacture of liquor is exclusively under dominion control you can ration materials that may be used for this purpose. They have done so in Britain and Australia. . . .
(2)	You can restrict the amount of liquor released from bond for sale. That would eliminate large wasteful expenditures. . . .
(3)	You could to-morrow commandeer distilleries for the manufacture of industrial alcohol so useful in making smokeless powder and as a basis for synthetic rubber. And you could order that a major part of liquor stocks now in existence be turned into industrial alcohol. Mr. Roosevelt has moved in this direction. . . .
The minister should give an answer to these three suggestions which have been advanced by the Canadian Temperance Federation. Another complaint we are hearing is that the brewers and distillers are having no difficulty in getting priority for the material required to expand their plants. I do not know whether or not that is the case, but I have had complaints to that effect from Vancouver, and the people resent it very strongly. Many people have the feeling that the distilling and brewing interests are being protected by the government, and it is most unwise that anything should be done which would give grounds for that belief. I think the whole situation can be fairly summed up by this expression, that Canadians cannot drink their way to victory. When sugar and gasoline are being rationed; when people cannot get fuel oil for their furnaces, and all this sort of thing, it does seem unreasonable that- restrictions cannot be placed on the sale of liquor.

For some weeks or months past I have been receiving letters in connection with this liquor question; therefore I do not feel that I should keep my chair warm this afternoon and let this opportunity go by without having at least a few words to say.
It may seem rather strange to some hon. members that I, who come from old Ireland, should say anything against liquor, but any-

thing I have to say this afternoon will be against it. I lived in Ireland for almost twenty years, and during that time I saw a great deal of suffering and misery caused by this liquor traffic. The situation here is exactly as it was in the old country. I think if we went around this or any other city of Canada to-day or any other day we could see some of the effects of this curse, and if this government is going to fulfil its duty to the men overseas, and their parents and relatives here in Canada, it should do something in the matter. We find that the government has interfered with provincial rights in other matters perhaps not quite so vital as this, and personally I believe that if the government does its duty now it will accede to at least some of the requests of the temperance association and various church organizations all over this country. Not many days ago I received a letter from a man in Edmonton which reads in part as follows:
Any person who reads the financial papers or even the stock market reports of the daily press knows that according to the report of Mr. E. P. Taylor-we presumed the one-dollar-a-year man (see Saturday Night, February 21, 1942), that Canadian Breweries cancelled the arrears of $6.75 per share and substituted a dividend rate of $3.40 per annum instead of $3 per share. The result of this may be seen in the increase in the stock from $40 to $46.76 per share. Hiram Walker-Gooderham and Vvorts, and Hiram Walker and Sons Distilleries Incorporated, according to a notice which appeared in the Olole and Mail of Toronto, May 13, 1941, redeemed $207,000 principal of' ten year four and one-quarter convertible debentures due December 1, 1945, on June 1, 1941, at 102J per cent of their principal amount with accrued interest on principal amount to said redemption date.
The letter goes on to say:
Many of our sons are entering His Majesty's-forces for $1.30 a day.
And a little further on he says:
Perhaps some of you members could pass on the information to Mr. Gibson and have him or his department ascertain if this $207,000 and $6.75 arrears per share was deducted from the excess profits tax of these companies who-are exempt from tne rationing system of some of the essentials, and if so see that the tax be refunded to the nation.
I believe in this country we have a number of habitual drinkers, and it is going to be pretty hard for them to break off that habit. Why should young men who are leaving home for the first time to enter his majesty's forces be encouraged by us to take up this habit? Why should we do these things for the advantage of certain companies who are said to occupy preferred positions with respect to rubber and other commodities? Why should our young men and women be faced1 with this traffic which in manv instances will ruin their

Excise Act Amendment
lives? I have two boys at home, and I expect that before long they will be going out among the rest of them. I certainly do not want to see them and the sons of other fathers and mothers tempted with this drug and traffic which could easily be done away with if proper precautions were taken.

I should like to say something about the remarks of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) and the correspondence he has received in connection with the taxation of liquor interests. A great many loose statements have been made outside this house with regard to this taxation. A question was asked some time ago by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) as to whether brewers and distillers have been permitted to pay arrears of dividends and redeem debentures out of their excess profits. This question was answered, but it did not seem to give satisfaction to some people outside the house. I have had one or two abusive letters in that connection and these were followed by an editorial in the United Church Observer, to which I replied but which has not received publicity. The matter has come up again and I think this is the reason for the letter received by the hon. member for Battle River. All brewers and distillers are required to pay their income and excess profits taxes before making any distribution out of earnings for any other purpose. Consequently any distribution that may be made is not made at the expense of any taxation that may be levied upon them.
That is the law.

Furthermore, reference is continually being made to Hiram Walker's. The company actually referred to is Hiram Walker and Sons Inc., which did redeem some 4f per cent debentures, I understand to an extent of 8207,000. This particular company is a subsidiary of Hiram Walker-Gooderham and Worts; it is a United States corporation, does business in the United States, and does not file an income tax return in Canada. This is the company quoted as an example of a corporation in Canada escaping taxation. It is most misleading, and the public are entitled to know the facts.
Do they pay an income tax in this country for the business they do here?
I understand that this company does not do business in this country. It is a United States company doing business in the United States.

Or any of its
subsidiaries?
44561-262i
It is a subsidiary of Hiram Walker-Gooderham and Worts, which is a Canadian company.

I had not intended speaking on this, resolution, but there are one or two facts I should like to point out to the committee and there is a suggestion I wish to make. The minister is always looking for suggestions in this connection, and I think this one will come within the province of his own department. The liquor bill for 1942 is estimated at $250,000,000. Investment income in 1937 amounted to $451,000,000, and in 1941, to $512,000,000. We shall be spending in this country for alcoholic beverages almost half the total investment income in 1941. I have never been a believer that prohibition would be effective in this countiy, but I have always deplored the moral and economic waste which goes along with the overconsumption of alcoholic beverages. The taste for alcohol is acquired, unfortunately quite easily by some, and the acquisition of that taste is stimulated on eveiy hand by the advertising of the liquor companies. To some extent advertising comes within the province of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson).
In Ontario there is a law against the advertising of liquor. WTe believe that the advertising of liquor is just as effective as advertising in other fields. We feel that the delights, if you want to call them that, or the pleasures of drinking should not be put before the young people of our province at every turn. However, since the war, there has been an evasion of this regulation by the beverage companies in Ontario. Advertising is now done under the guise of its being a contribution to the war effort. We see "buy war savings certificates", or "$4 will make $5", and advertising of that kind by the beverage companies. As long as a certain small por.tion of the advertisement is devoted to patriotic purposes, these companies may advertise. It is called a patriotic advertisement rather than an advertisement of liquor.
I suppose that all these companies are in the excess profits tax bracket, so that this advertising is virtually being paid for by the people of Canada. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the statute should provide that for the period of the war the liquor companies shall not be allowed to advertise their products in any province. In that way greater revenue will be provided for his department, and there will not be an incentive placed before the youth of this country to drink more and more and thus acquire a taste for alcohol.
Excise Act Amendment

There is another point which was not mentioned by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth). He said that we are dealing with fiscal returns and not with morals, that we should not concern ourselves with the consumption of liquor. But we must remember something which has been brought out by other hon. members, namely, that the liquor trade consumes many products and services which would otherwise be useful. I am strongly against any increase in this trade being brought about by means of advertising.

With respect to advertising, I may say that these companies are not allowed to increase their advertising costs. These costs are being rigidly controlled by the income tax department. This refers not only to liquor advertising but to all advertising. Strict limitations are being imposed on advertising expenses as compared with the pre-war average.
What about this so-called patriotic advertising by distillers and brewers? Are they allowed for that?

We did allow an increase up to 10 per cent additional; that is, 10 per cent over the pre-war average advertising rate. This was done for one war loan campaign, but it has since been discontinued. Any advertising must in general be within the pre-war advertising expenditure average.

It might seem like discrimination against the liquor industry if we were to prohibit them from advertising and not allow them to deduct this expense as an operating cost. However, I do not believe that this discrimination is unfair since in this resolution we are imposing an extra tax on the beverage trade because it is a beverage trade and not just a general industry. I see no reason why the minister should not give serious consideration to asking the beverage companies to eliminate advertising for the remainder of the war.

I still believe we should endeavour to get a true picture of the whole thing and not allow distortions to go out from this house to the country in connection with this set-up. It seems to me that the quantity of labour and materials used is the important thing and not the total liquor bill. Can the minister give me the information I asked for a short time ago in connection with that aspect of the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is right. It does not
include the customs duty on the liquor imported. I have not the figures of the total sales within Canada, and I do not know just how they could be obtained. It would be simple enough to get the figures of the sales of the liquor commissions, but then there are the hotels, beverage rooms, wine shops, and so forth. The total figures are not available, and as far as I know they are not procurable.
Would not the total amount obtained by producers from sales in Canada be available?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I do not know. Several of
these companies carry on a soft-drink business as well as an alcoholic beverage business, and an export business too.
There is one point which perhaps I should mention. One may be misled by the huge figures one sees connected with the names of certain distilleries, such as Seagram's, Distillers Corporation, and so forth. Some of these distilling companies do most of their business in the United States, and yet all their business appears in the financial statements published in the papers. Those figures could be separated easily enough.
Before the minister leaves that point, would the figures of the eight liquor commissions not give the total sales to the public?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, because they would
leave out the beverage rooms, hotels and wine shops, which do not purchase from the commission, and which would make a very large total.

Even
without that, do not the sales of the provincial liquor commissions amount to a shockingly large sum? I wish the minister would deal with the larger question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the sales are going
up pretty fast and that people are quite justified in being concerned, but the point is what to do about it. I have received a great many letters, so much so that I have felt that I am being manipulated into the position of being defender of the status quo in dealing with a lot of people who have written me from all over Canada. But it is not much use just to talk about the increase in the consumption of liquo-r without putting forward some constructive policy to deal with the situation. I have listened this afternoon for suggestions, and there have been some.
The most obvious one would be rationing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but I was beginning
with the suggestion of the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), who suggested that we stop advertising. That might be of some small effect.
They put a terrific value on it, judging by the amount of advertising they do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But there are two values in advertising. First, it may increase the consumption of the product, or second, it may increase the consumption of one's own product at the expense of that of some competitor. Without knowing anything in particular about the matter, my judgment would tell me that the chief reason why the brewers and distillers advertise is to bring their own brand to the attention of the consumer so that he will drink theirs instead of the other fellow's.

That is not why we
eliminated advertising in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know what the
experience was in Ontario, but it may be that that would be the chief result of the elmina-tion of advertising.
Take Nova Scotia, a great province, I need hardly say. I have been reading the report of the speech of the hon. member for Mackenzie, and according to the figures he gave the percentage increase in Nova Scotia was greater than that in any other province. It was 35 per cent, as compared with 27 per cent for New Brunswick, and so forth. There may have been a reason for that-the war activity, the naval activity, the merchant shipping activity, and so forth in Nova Scotia, but I would point out that in that province you
have a government headed by a prohibitionist. Perhaps I am taking liberties in saying that about Mr. MacMillan, but certainly if there is in public life an enemy of the liquor traffic I have always thought it was the premier of Nova Scotia. As a result, I think, of that fact the government of Nova Scotia has sharply curtailed hours of sale. I do not know what the situation now is, but I do not think they sell liquor after six o'clock in the evenings, or on Saturdays at all. They have no beverage rooms, nor will they permit the beverage system to be introduced. In fact a great deal of unfavourable publicity was given to the government of that province not long ago over a club which they closed there.
So there you have a government which is going, undoubtedly, just as far as public sentiment will permit it to go, under the impetus of a sincere desire to curtail the sale of liquor; and you have a 35 per cent increase there, higher than that in any other province.
The delegation whose representatives I heard presented four requests. The first was that liquor stores be closed at ten o'clock at night; or perhaps it was eight o'clock; the next, that no advertising of liquor be permitted; the third was that the beverage rooms be closed, and the fourth was that when the beverage rooms were closed there should be no wet canteen.
Two of those conditions already exist in Nova Scotia with, as far as anyone can see, no effect whatever in curtailing the consumption of liquor. I have never been able to understand why anyone had any ground for thinking that if the dominion entered the provincial fields and sought to superimpose dominion regulations on provincial regulations, the dominion would get any better results. No one advocates dominion prohibition; no one in any of the provinces where liquor is sold advocates provincial prohibition; and the view we have taken is that the regulation of the sale of liquor is a provincial responsibility. It is true, I think, that the crown in the right, of the dominion could, under the War Measures Act, step in and regulate the crown in the right of the province. It would be a most disagreeable and friction-creating departure, I think, for the crown in the right of the dominion to undertake it; nevertheless, I think it has the statutory power. But. is there any reason to think that the crown in the right of the province or the government of a province is not doing its duty as it sees it within the bounds which are set by public sentiment in the various provinces?

What about the suggestions of the Canadian Temperance Federation, contained in that advertisement?
