speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I am not in a position to argue those. I would have to give some thought to them, and I should not be asked to argue about them here. If I do improvise arguments, it may be held that I am going to great lengths to repel suggestions by wellmeaning, patriotic citizens. But it occurred to me as the hon. member was reading them that the first suggestion, namely, that materials be rationed, will not affect the production of some spirits for two years, and of other spirits for four or more years. The spirits which are being consumed are being taken out of storage. There is a large amount of spirits already in storage, and the effect of rationing barley and other grains would be felt only in the fairly distant future.
What about beer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The situation will be different as regard's beer; the effects will be felt in two or three months. The policy which is being asked for is to create in the country a scarcity of beer and spirits, not to ration a product of which there is a scarcity on account of inescapable reasons, but to create a scarcity; and while it might work out all right, I would certainly think there would be the most awful time here with bootlegging that was ever had in any country.
Just why, now?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Because there is plenty of
raw material left out of which to distil and to brew.

You are
talking about home brew?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The excise department is
not out of the woods so far as the moonshine problem is concerned: it is seizing stills right along, and illicit distilling is going on just the same as it ever did. Hon. members today have talked about this not being a measure of curtailment, but a revenue measure. Well, it probably is primarily a revenue measure, although I want to remind the committee that last year hon. members were urging a higher tax on spirits and on malt, not as a revenue producer but as a method of curtailment.

I do not
recall that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes. The hon. member for Mackenzie and others were urging it on that ground.

The public, urged it.
I Mr. Green.]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, the public urged it.
I have been attacked and the government has been attacked from a hundred quarters because of our alleged tenderness toward the liquor interests in regard to taxation.
The government's love for the liquor interests.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: What is the rate in the United Kingdom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The rate in the United Kingdom is terribly high.
That is for domestic consumption, but not for export. There is no rate at all on liquor for export.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Has the minister the rates for New Zealand or Australia?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not the rates for New Zealand or Australia. It must be remembered that a province has what is essentially a rate of taxation. It is a profit, but it is money taken by the provinces considerably in excess of the cost of carrying on the business. In effect it is a tax. Undoubtedly the provinces will charge a profit on the increase in the cost of liquor which has come about as a result of these higher taxes.
It must be remembered that in England they have no taxes on the exported article, and that is a big part of their trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

As I
understand it, there is no revenue from liquor manufactured in the United Kingdom and exported all over the world. That is

Excise Act Amendment
what they have to sell. The situation in England to-day is that their whisky costs about a dollar a quart more than it does here.
I am rather disappointed that the minister does not feel that there is any responsibility on this government. We have a large increase in the national revenue. That is going out to all and sundry, much of it to the people who are spending it on beer and hard liquor. I have felt that a larger proportion of that national income which is now going to the liquor trade and the provincial governments ought to be switched to the war effort; and the only method adopted by the government here is to raise the excise and the import duty by $2 a gallon. I have no doubt that that will bring in the amount of the estimated increase of revenue which the minister suggests, but it will not deal with what is now a pressing problem.
The minister says we shall have to leave the matter to the provinces. Well, notwithstanding the certificate of character he has given Mr. MacMillan, I am afraid that gentleman is in the same position as most of the other provincial governments. They need the money and this is the easiest possible way in which to get it. If that is the position the minister takes, it is too bad. This government undoubtedly has a great deal of power to deal with this matter. You can ration the amount of Scotch and Irish whisky that *will be imported from the old country. There is no question about our power to do that. You can ration the amount that the provincial liquor commissions will be able to sell, and you can limit the amount the distillers shall "take out of bond. It is all held in bond until the excise duty is paid. This government has power to ration in a very large way, not to say that a man shall be able to buy only three bottles of liquor or one bottle of liquor a week, as they did in Newfoundland, which would be in effect putting a restriction on the liquor commissions and therefore on the provinces, because the commissions are simply agencies created by the provincial governments. This government, I repeat, has a great deal of power which it could use to cut down the consumption of liquor in Canada. The minister says that would immediately revive the bootlegger. I will tell him that in my province there is little illicit distilling going on. The day of the home brewer is pretty largely gone. They have been dealt with pretty severely in the past.
Maybe you don't get around among them.

I confess I do not. I have not had anything much to do with anything of that sort for a long time. The only bootlegging I know of that ever went on in New Brunswick-and it did for a good many years-was the bootlegging on the part of people who bought commission liquor and sold it after hours. We do not have liquor stores open in the evening, no beer and wine stores, and I hope we never shall. But the bootlegging that goes on is winked at. I took occasion to call up the chief liquor commissioner himself and I told him about a particular case. What was the answer? He said, "You will have to produce the evidence to me." I replied, "I am going a long way when I call attention to this and I am certainly not going to be a detective for you. I give you the name of the party who is doing the bootlegging and you can go after him." I also called up the chief of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, who was responsible for the enforcement of the liquor law in New Brunswick. The mounted police have taken over the whole service. Complaint had been made to me with respect to an individual in a certain village some distance from the city of Fredericton who was bootlegging commission liquor, not after hours, but at any time, because there is just one liquor store in the whole of the county of York. I saw to it, that as far as I was concerned no liquor stores would be opened in any other place in the community except Fredericton, and the present provincial government observed that.
How many bootleggers are there, besides the store?
Not many.
How do you know?

I do not know personally. The hon. member puts the question to me and cross-examines me, but I cannot give definite information. I can say, however, that the illicit bootlegging has been very limited. When I put the matter to the commissioner of mounted police, he said, "What evidence have you?" I answered, "It is not my place to get evidence; it is your business to get it when I tell you it is available. All you have to do is to send a plainclothes man to a certain place and you will get the evidence." He did so and the fellow spent the next Christmas in gaol where he ought to have been. That is the kind of bootlegging there is in New Brunswick, the bootlegger who operates after hours, and it is very limited.
I believe the minister would get cooperation from New Brunswick. Public sentiment there
Excise Act Amendment

is such as would compel the commission to make it harder to get liquor. I am alarmed about the evidence I see of sales to young soldiers. That is what is on my soul to-day. I went into Fredericton a week ago on Saturday afternoon. I got home at noon, or before noon, and on Saturday afternoon there was a continuous procession of young men in uniform going to and coming from the liquor commission store. It was mostly beer, I should judge, but they were carrying it by the dozen. That is where I think the huge increase has been, because in our part of the country we have no war industry and no large increase from the national revenue. The principal part is in connection with young soldiers. It is, I admit, a problem. At the training centre Colonel Brooks does not allow a wet canteen, but across the way a block distant there is a wet canteen. And there is complaint. In one place you can get beer and in the other place you cannot, so that anyone who does not feel responsible throws up his hands and says, "Let it go; it is not my funeral; it is not my obligation." I try to deal with the matter from the larger point of view as a national problem. Here is vast consumption of liquor. I think something should be done, and this government can do something. First of all, I suggest negotiation with the provincial governments to see if something cannot be done to reduce the huge quantities that are sold. An hon. member says something about advertising. I have noticed a magazine called the New World, filled with gorgeous advertising of liquor put out by certain interests close to the brewing interests. If you want to be fair about Mr. Taylor, and the dollar-a-year men, he has not been a dollar-a-year man for some time. I ran that story down, and I was satisfied that the beer shipped to Libya was shipped as a result of a request from overseas. They could not ship it from Britain. The soldiers think they have to have their beer in Libya. The British Tommy says he must have it; he will not be deprived of it. Some people look on beer as food; here it is a beverage, not a food at all. Perhaps it is the soldier's luxury. I am not so much concerned about the consumption of beer as I am about the consumption of hard spirits. I think we could get along without that in this countiy. It could be drastically reduced with beneficial consequences. The minister himself has some responsibility. I am not going to make an issue of this matter, and probably I have said more than I intended to when I rose, but I do think something must be done. The situation must be grappled with, and this government has a responsibility. Certainly the

provincial governments have their responsibilities, and perhaps the public discussion here will focus attention on the matter. The publicity from this debate will probably show to the provincial governments that, so far as there has been an expression of opinion in this house, we are nearly all in agreement here. The problem should be grappled with; the duty is partly on this government and partly on the provincial governments.

I do not know if I
have much to add to this discussion. I was in at the earlier part of the discussion, and I think I agree pretty much with what the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Mackenzie and others said. But while the discussion was good in itself there was not much in the way of constructive suggestions as to how the consumption of liquor might be reduced. I do not think it is strange that there should be a large increase in the consumption of liquor at this time, because where large aggregations of people meet and have little to do except try to amuse themselves, it is quite understandable that there would be a large increase in the consumption of liquor.
After thinking about this matter or being in a position where I could think about it for many years, and having been at one time a believer in prohibition, I am now almost convinced that people who want to curtail the consumption of liquor are attacking the problem from the wrong angle. They are attacking it from the moral point of view, but I do not think we shall ever get anywhere in that way. I believe that a great deal could be done to-day if the matter were attacked from the health point of view. The people of this country to-day are becoming generally healthconscious. I believe that the harmfulness of drinking liquor could be emphasized in that way, w-ith a regular campaign of education carried on to show the young men and young women the harmful effects of liquor. As I go home along Bank street every evening I pass a certain hotel about a quarter past eleven o'clock when the people are coming out, and it is a common occurrence to see young men and young women coming out drunk and falling against the wall. Anything that could be done to put a stop to that should be done. I am satisfied, however, that it cannot be done by prohibition or by dealing with the matter from the moral point of view.
A few years ago I had the good fortune to be able to make a visit to Europe, and I was astonished to see how common it was to have liquor in every eating-place, even in the northern cities, the Scandinavian cities.

Excise Act Amendment
It seemed to me that there was less drunkenness than one sees in this country. I believe our system of beer parlours is one of the worst possible ways of dispensing of liquors.
I think it would be a good thing if light wines were served in restaurants rather than that people should have to go to a beer parlour and sit down and swill beer without anything much else to attract their attention, except the rather second-rate conversation that goes on. I agree with the hon. member for Rose-dale that advertising should be reduced. But along with that there should be a health compaign teaching people the harmful effects of liquor. This would do much more to curtail the consumption than anything else.
I noticed in the papers to-day that the director of national selective service says that non-essential industries may have to close down because he says some 250,000 workers will be needed within the next five months. Among the non-essential industries that could be restricted are those of brewing and distilling.

Has the minister given any mnsideration to making a direct appeal to \he Canadian people? There is no doubt that much of the money that is spent on liquor could be spent for bonds and war savings certificates. When there was a shortage of sugar an appeal was made to the people to restrict its use, and the same with gasoline. Of course both were eventually rationed. But it might be helpful if an appeal were made to cut down the consumption of liquor. I am sure thousands would listen to that appeal if it were put forward with the authority that a government appeal would carry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The suggestion is worthy of consideration. I do not know how far my duties go in regard to such appeals, but perhaps the government-
The minister should ask the people to spend the money on war savings certificates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but I am pretty careful not to select particular commodities, unless on economic grounds; by that I mean with a view to saving and making available specific materials, such as steel, for example. The saving here would be very little. As the hon. member for Vancouver East said, the impetus behind the drive here is a moral impetus for the most part, it is persons who believe in prohibition, who have done so for years past, now coming forward-
That is very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. They now come forward and say, "You should now have prohibition or curtailment, whatever may have been the case in time of peace." The suggestion of the hon. member can be considered; that is all I can say.

This matter is, I think, indirectly concerned with the budget.
I do not think any hon. member feels that it is specifically a matter for the Minister of Finance. It is a matter for the government.
I think we all realize that the use of liquor cannot be done away with. You cannot, by taxation, stop people from drinking liquor, although you may be able to curtail the amount used. I think we must recognize that the sale of liquor cannot be legislated out of existence or regulated out of existence.
There are, however, some facts of which I believe the government-not particularly the Minister of Finance-should take cognizance. We have been shown this afternoon the comparatively great increase in the amount of money spent on liquor. As has been said, that is probably to be expected. Whether it is or not, many of the best people in this country are worried about it. They are not necessarily teetotallers or churchgoers, but the people who constitute the backbone of society in this country are worried about the situation in regard to the use of liquor during war time.
The second factor is that no one for a moment believes that the federal government cannot control liquor if it so desires. In view of the controls that have been exercised by the government in relation to human necessities, it is simply useless to tell the general public that the federal government has not power to control this industry if it so desires.
The third factor I think the government should take into consideration is an idea which I find very widespread in the community from which I come; that is, the idea that in some way the government is protecting the liquor interests. I have no reason to believe that is true; I have no proof, any more than anyone else has, but there is the opinion abroad to-day among the thinking people of this country that the government is supporting and protecting the liquor interests, and that is bad for the morale of the people.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made a suggestion which I thought was extremely important. Within the past six months I have noticed that in the city of Toronto, in nearly every street car, in our buses and on our billboards, the most captivating signs supporting the war effort bear underneath them the name of some brewery. I believe in Ontario we have a law that prohibits liquor advertising.
Excise Act Amendment

but everywhere in the city of Toronto you will find the most captivating, interesting and artistic advertising put out in the interests of the war effort bearing the names and addresses of some breweries. I think that is uncalled for. It is annoying to a great mass of well-intentioned, patriotic citizens, and I believe that is something to which the government might well pay attention.
I do not know what can be done by way of control. I think if control or rationing is applied it will have to be done with reason, because I am convinced that this is a matter which must be studied. No one in this country, even the most ardent temperance advocates, would like a return to bootlegging on i large scale; and I think any control or rationing should be not so much from the moral point of view but rather, as has been suggested, as a war effort. The hon. member for Waterloo South spoke of the amount of money spent on liquor, of the amount that went for material, for labour, and so on. The point there, it seems to me, is that most of these materials, most of that labour, all the rubber and gasoline used in the distribution of these goods, are required to-day for more essential war purposes, and I think it is on this basis that we should appeal to our public. Certainly the suggestion is sound that any effort in this direction should be accompanied by an educational programme. I have yet to see any information emanating from the department of public information urging people to be patriotic and drink less beer, or anything along that line. I think it only reasonable to suppose that a great many of our people, if they could be shown that the consumption of beer during war time is unpatriotic, would bring about a voluntary reduction in that consumption without need for much government regulation. I believe a programme of that kind would contribute materially to our war effort, at least as much as a great deal of the information being sent out by that department.

Is it the attitude of
the government in connection with this tax on spirituous liquors and malt and beer that they are taxing a luxury, or do they look upon this as a source of revenue, or is the tax intended to curtail civilian expenditure on nonessential goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it would be a combination of all those factors.

Does the government
consider, then, that malt and liquors are a luxury, and that beer is a luxury in exactly the same way? I see that the increases are approximately the same. The increase on

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The beer tax mentioned by the hon. member I feel sure must be very unimportant. The important tax is the duty on malt, which is increased from 12 cents to 16 cents per pound.

And how about the
attitude of the government with regard to spirituous liquors?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I find it hard to define an
attitude in precise language.

Well, would you call
spirituous liquors a luxury?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be a matter for the individual; he can decide what he wants to call it.

Does the minister not think that these increased taxes on liquor and malt will bring into effect the law of diminishing returns?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think they will cut consumption down a great deal. I would not mind if it could be cut down to some extent.
However, there is so much money in the hands of the public that the law of diminishing returns does not operate very powerfully. There will be more results from the increased income tax.

C. That the duty of excise on Canadian raw leaf tobacco when sold for consumption be increased from ten cents to twenty cents per pound actual weight.

I am a little bit exercised over this increase in the excise duty on raw leaf tobacco. A lot of flue-cured tobacco is grown in Ontario, particularly in the southern counties, and a considerable industry has grown up. For some time we have been growing what is known as Burley tobacco in considerable quantities. This industry brings in a good deal of money to the farmers in three or four counties along the shores of lake Erie, and I am just wondering whether this increase in duty will not have some effect on prices paid to producers. At the present time prices paid for tobacco are determined every fall at a conference between a certain producers' association and the processors, and I am afraid that this increase will perhaps give a handle to the processors to beat down the price to the producers. There is not only an increase in the excise on raw leaf tobacco; there is also an increase of one cent per five cigarettes, 25 per cent on cigars and a cent per pound or part of a cent per pound on manufactured tobacco.
Excise Act Amendment

I should like to have an assurance from the minister that this increase is not going to interfere with the price the producer will realize.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This item would not apply to the sales of which the hon. gentleman is speaking. Those sales are not to the consumer.

They are to the manufacturer, but the ultimate effect is that the cost of the raw materials to the manufacturer is increased, and he will try to take it out of the primary producer if he can. While I do not know whether the price ceiling applies to tobacco or not, there will be an attempt to try to keep the price-ceiling structure level all along the line, and I would be fearful that this increase would come out of the primary producer. That is what has happened in other lines of endeavour, and I am afraid that we shall see history repeating itself.
There is another matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the committee. There is an increase of 100 per cent in the tax on raw leaf tobacco. That appears to be a very steep increase in comparison with the excise tax on cigars, cigarettes and manufactured tobaccos which are dealt with under resolutions 9, 10 and 19 of the Special War Revenue Act. This raises an interesting point. Heretofore cigarettes and manufactured tobacco have been taxable only under the Excise Act, and an excise duty has been levied rather than an excise tax. Now it is proposed that in addition to the excise duty on cigarettes and manufactured tobacco, levied under the Excise Act, there shall be levied an excise tax under the Special War Revenue Act. I should think that there would be confusion as a result of that action, and I think the minister is called upon to justify the confusion which will unquestionably result from the introduction of this new principle in the taxation of tobacco and cigarettes. I would have thought that simplicity, ease of collection, efficiency of audit and such considerations would dictate that the increases should be increased in duty under the Excise Act rather than the imposition of new taxes under the Special War Revenue Act. I wonder whether the minister's action in this regard, imposing a new tax rather than an increased duty, has anything to do with the maintenance of the price ceiling. I would assume that that is correct, but I doubt very much whether any such considerations outweigh the disadvantages which will, in my opinion, accrue from levying an excise duty and an excise tax upon the same commodities. It is axiomatic that an

excise duty is a much simpler and easier means of taxing any commodity than an excise tax.
I believe that there are now two branches of the excise division of the Department of National Revenue, the excise duty branch and the excise tax branch. Will there not be duplication and overlapping in the administration of the new proposals? I would have thought it would be much more satisfactory if the means had been adopted of increasing the duty in preference to imposing the new tax. I think the minister ought to justify this change.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The administration is by the same division of the Department of National Revenue. It is administered by the commissioner of excise. I do not think there will be any duplication. It was considered desirable to keep the new tax separate in every way from the excise duty.. The excise duty is reckoned in the price of cigarettes for priceceiling purposes. The new tax is a separate tax, announced to be on a different basis, and not to be reckoned in the price of the article for price-ceiling purposes.
So as to preserve the sanctity of the price ceiling- just another dodge to preserve it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the word "dodge"' is objectionable.
All right- another example of the trial and error method.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We thought it was desirable to put a tax on the cigarettes in the box. It is a stamp tax applicable to the cigarettes in the box. While the tax is collected from the manufacturer, it is easily identifiable as being a separate tax imposed by this budget. It has been announced that it has nothing to do with the price-ceiling policy.

It is imposed in this way so that the price of cigarettes will not be further raised beyond the actual amount of the tax. That is the real truth of the matter. But what care is the minister going to take to see that the primary producer gets as much after this tax of 10 cents is imposed as he got before?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The tax of 10 cents on raw leaf tobacco does not apply at all to raw leaf sold to manufacturers. It applies to raw leaf which is sold to consumers, and which comes into competition with manufactured tobacco. The logical thing to have done would have been to increase the dirty by the same number

It certainly would have to be increased 10 cents to preserve the competitive situation between sellers of raw leaf to consumers and sellers of manufactured tobacco to consumers.
How much revenue does the minister expect to derive from resolution No. 6 of the Excise Act? How much raw leaf tobacco is sold for consumption?

Last year we collected

3.	That there shall be imposed, levied and collected an excise tax of twenty-five cents per month on each telephone extension in any dwelling house, apartment or other domestic establishment.

I think
this is absolutely the meanest tax of the lot, and I am going to ask the minister to take it off. The extension of a telephone in a house is usually for the purpose of saving the feet of the housewife or the maid. The telephone companies charge for this service, and they charge too much. The mechanical apparatus does not cost very much. They charge, I think, 50 cents a month. This makes the cost 75 cents a month. That is a substantial tax on each telephone user, for a telephone which is installed, perhaps, for the convenience of aged people. A telephone in the house has now become a necessity. I am opposed to this tax. I do not know what the minister is going to get out of it, but of all the mean taxes that ever were imposed by parliament, this is, I think, the meanest. It is not imposed on business. In my business office we have five or six extensions: one makes money out of these telephones; a man absorbs the cost as part of his business expense. But this is a tax on a telephone which is put in to save one's wife from running up and down stairs. I suggest to the minister that he withdraw it. It is the only one I will ask him to take off. How much shall we lose if we do not impose this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The estimated revenue for
the full year is $125,000; for the remainder of the year, $90,000.

Well, the
minister will lose that much, probably three times as much, through the resentment of the housewives of this country. The women will say, "I am not going to buy any more war savings certificates if I have to take out my extension.

speechtext: Surely not.

Oh, well,
they will take it out, human nature being what it is. The minister is making a mistake in imposing that tax.
You are right.
I have never heard from the telephone companies that it was their desire to do away with these extensions. They are always asking people to put them in.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, no, there is a shortage
of instruments.

That is
only a temporary condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It is a mean tax, and I am against it.
When the minister made the announcement of the tax in the house, he said, "I don't care whether they leave them in or whether they take them out."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not say that.

It is a tax on a
tax: that is what it is. If you are going to have a tax on these extensions in business we shall have to take them out, and some revenue will be lost. After all, however, look at the matter from this point of view. Things are being made more difficult for people all the time; everybody has to cut dow-n on household expenditures and so on, and now a wife in a family who had two maids and now has only one, or who had one maid and now has none at all, needs the extension for use while she is upstairs doing her job. It is only a small tax as far as that is concerned1-twenty-five cents a month-but I think it is a disgraceful one. If there is a need of telephone instruments to be installed some place else, tell the public that you have to have them, and then you can obtain them from houses where there are twro or three, or other places where there are more telephones than are needed. I ask the minister to take out this tax, or he will lose more revenue than he will ever gain.
I agree wTith the leader of the opposition that this is a mean tax, but I would like to ask the minister what tax is not mean.

The tax
on whisky!
There is one class of people whom this is not going to touch, and that is the class that cannot afford a telephone at all. There are quite a number of people who cannot afford a telephone.
Not many now.

The other thing that bothers me is this, if we cancel a number of these

Special War Revenue Act
items where will the minister get his revenue? If I suggest that a tax should be taken off I should try to suggest some compensatory tax.

In
answer to the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, I have letters on my desk upstairs from three families who cannot afford telephones, but they have them in the house owing to the fact that there are in the house bedridden invalids who need telephones. They pay 55 cents a month for the extension, and with this extra tax of S3 a year it will mean that S9.60 has to be paid for extension service which is necessary as well as giving a little pleasure to the invalid. The downstairs telephone is, of course, required, and many a time during the past year it has been necessary to call the doctor. I suggest that the minister cancel this tax.

The hon. member who has just resumed his seat has partly expressed what I rose to say in the first place. This is really a tax on a luxury, and to invoke the name of the housewife, with all the sympathy there is for her, is certainly not an argument, because 95 per cent of them have no telephone in the house at all. There is no necessity for a telephone in every room, and therefore the tax is a proper one, with this exception. There are homes in Canada-not so many of them, but there are some where I think there should be an exemption; that is, where there is an extension for the use of someone who is bedridden. But there is no blanket argument on the ground that it is a benefit to the housewife or that it is a necessity, because it certainly is not.
I support what the hon. member says in favour of an exemption for invalids.
As I read this resolution, it applies only to dwelling houses, apartments and other domestic establishments and is not a tax on an extension in any business concern.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

How about a professional man, for instance a doctor, who has his office and residence in the same building and has an extension for the convenience of himself and his patients at night? Does it apply in such a situation? The extension is paid for and well paid for, and it is a convenience not only to the professional man himself but to his clientele.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not consider that taxable. It is part of the professional establishment and not a part of the domestic establishment as such.

Would the minister consider the question in regard to invalids, to whom a telephone is a necessity? Surely it is as much a necessity to a bedridden person as it is to a doctor. We would appreciate a statement from the minister as to whether he will consider that question. In 95 per cent of cases it is a luxury and should be taxed, but for the bedridden person the telephone is a source of comfort not only personally but to those on whom that person depends.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would not care to make an exception for such a small proportion of such a small tax. It would hardly be worth doing so. Moreover, it would be administratively difficult to draw the line between invalids and semi-invalids and those who are not invalids at all.
And there are rich invalids and poor invalids.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We would get into all sorts of difficulty.

I support my leader's contention with regard to the tax. It is not only a mean tax but also a nuisance tax. I do not think this house has sufficient sympathy with people who are now burdened with larger than six-roomed houses which they cannot get rid of because there is no market for them. Such people cannot adapt themselves very readily to the more restricted circumstances in keeping with their incomes after taxation, and they may have two telephones. With the present shortage of domestic help it means more work for the women in that class. The tax is a nuisance. True, the amount is only $3 a year, but that is added to the charge which the telephone company makes and which, in my opinion, is and always has been exorbitant. One year's rental is about equal to the cost of the instrument, but now the minister sees a loophole to enable him to impose another tax. It is unfair. Many business men have extra telephones in their living rooms in order that they may conduct business, receiving calls in the evening, and that involves a business charge which they cannot take into account in their business expenses. A great many people who formerly had a good middle-class income are now reduced to a very small income by reason of taxation, and it has been necessary for them to maintain a certain standard of living in order to earn that income. Now the minister comes along with this picayune tax which is nothing but a nuisance. I think he would be well advised to take it off. At a more appropriate time I may make a suggestion as to where he could impose a better tax.
Special War Revenue Act

Why should there be a tax on a private telephone and not on a business telephone? One of the fundamental principles of taxation is ability to pay. A business is more capable of paying the tax than is a householder who has a telephone for the convenience of those in his home, and if it is purely a ' business proposition there are many reasons why the tax should be not on private telephones but on business telephones. The greatest percentage of extensions are for business reasons, but there are many other reasons than business for putting in an extension in a house. The difficulty of securing domestic help is one reason why the householder should have a telephone extension, and another reason is that there may be privacy in another room for business conversation. If the tax were intended to bring in revenue it would be better to put it on business rather than private telephones.

I wish to pursue further the question of exemption for invalids. I do not think the minister is right in regard to administrative difficulties in carrying out the exemption. The telephone company puts in the extension and knows the purpose for which it is required, and that is entered in the books of the company. In the United States the

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Whenever we seriously considered taxing railway passes-and we have discussed this matter a great deal-it has always been represented to me that free transportation was regarded by a great many people in this country as one of the conditions of their employment, part of their remuneration, and that if we were to step in and tax
415S
Special War Revenue Act

those passes there would be a tremendous storm of protest. I am willing to consider the matter if there is a widespread demand here in the house, but I am afraid that if I were to say now that we would turn round and tax free transportation, for one member who has asked for it ten would protest against it. I am also afraid that in regard to the taxation of passes of members of parliament, for one member from a distant point, such as the hon. member for New Westminster, who would be agreeable, there would be ten members from distant points who would say it was most unfair to tax them so much more than the members who live near Ottawa. These are some of the objections that would be offered to any tax on free transportation. Those who work for the railways have always considered . that free transportation was a condition attached to their employment. That is the point of view that has always come forward every time we have had this discussion, though I must say I have not had any representations from the men themselves. I am sure there would be a tremendous number of railway employees and members of parliament who would object to the taxation of free transportation.

I should like to point out one consideration with respect to the transportation of hon. members. A member of parliament does not travel on a pass which is issued as a favour by the railway. He travels free as a result of legislation of this parliament, which I think was placed upon the statute books to overcome the charge that he might be influenced by the railways in their handing out free transportation to him. Under this legislation he is under no obligation to them; in other words, he travels as a matter of right and not as a matter of favour. I think that is why the provision was placed in the Railway Act as long ago as 1917 or 1918. Those of us who have read the novel by Winston Churchill with regard to the abuses in the New Hampshire legislature in connection with free transportation will remember the revolution brought about by the publication of that novel. So much was that so that to-day there has been a great change in the handing out of free transportation in the United States. They are very much more restricted than we are; it is confined almost entirely to railway employees and their relatives.
With regard to railway employees I should say that from time immemorial the right of free transportation for the employees themselves, not only on their own line but, after a period of time, on other lines, rightly or wrongly is looked upon as part of the working
[Mr. Ilsley.)
conditions of the* railway men. Perhaps the railways are very generous in this respect, but I think you would have a little revolution on your hands if you were to tax these passes. These are among our most patriotic people, and if transportation facilities are being taxed to their capacity the railways have the remedy in their own hands. At the Christmas holiday, and other times when railway communications were being taxed to the utmost by the movement of men on furlough, the railways just informed certain classes of relatives of their employees that they would not honour passes between certain dates, and there was not a murmur about it. I think we can leave that matter in the hands of the railways. In justice to members of parliament, however, I wanted to point out the distinction, that we do not travel on the railways as a result of any favour from the railways. That section was placed in the Railway Act to abrogate what I might call the humiliation of accepting a favour from a railway company, or of being under any obligation to a railway company in the matter of transportation, leaving members of parliament free to travel as a matter of right.
I would have no objection to paying a fax on my railway transportation, but I tell the committee that it would be a very substantial sum during the course of a year. Members of the cabinet would not be in as bad a position, because the country would pay their travelling expenses, and properly so, since they are, as a rule, travelling on official business. Not many of them, at all events during these days, travel for pleasure; and the members travel on public business also. If a member goes home on Friday evening and comes back on Monday morning, to say that he should pay a 'tax is, I think, not fair. Let us be fair to ourselves. Surely we get enough knocks from the public as it is. I feel like defending members of parliament against the picayune charges that are sometimes levelled against them, not very often but from time to time. Somebody will say with a sneer, "Oh, he travels on a free pass." He does not travel on a free pass at all; he travels as a matter of right, so that he may be free from any suggestion that he is receiving a favour at the hands of a railway company. I know the hon. member for New Westminster is very sincere about this matter; he has advocated it a good many times, and there have been times when I have thought that the relatives of the railway employees took pretty generous advantage of the free transportation provision. But they have grown to understand that this is their right, and I think it would take a long process of education to disabuse

Special War Revenue Act
their minds in that regard. I am not going to urge that they be liable to payment of this tax; there are other ways of getting at them. They are a class of people who earn good money, and they will contribute to the war effort of this country.

I should like to add a word in this connection. With regard to railway employees, I am of the opinion that the provision of free transportation forms part of their salary or wages, and I share the view of the leader of the opposition that it would be very unfair to tax them. But I should like to say a word on behalf of those who must pay large sums for railway fares, those who travel long distances. I think the hon. member for Peterborough West made a good suggestion in that connection, to which we should pay attention. I think there should be a ceiling on this tax in regard to long trips.
The return fare from here to Vancouver is about $200, and the tax would amount to around S30. A man is punished for living so far away from Ottawa or from his business. I should like to say a word for the relatives of soldiers or for the soldiers themselves. A boy who has enlisted may have his home far away from the point of embarkation. A mother who happens to live in Vancouver may want to see her boy in Halifax before he leaves, and I think a case Like this should be exempted from the tax. I raise my humble voice to join with other hon. members and ask that something be done.

The minister is here entering into the field of a retail purchase tax. Heretofore we have
been clear of that type of tax. It resembles in its limited sphere a turn-over tax. I wonder how such a thing as this is going to be checked up. It will require a whole army of auditors to check up on this tax. Would it not be better to confine it, as we have to-day, to the manufacturer? I do not see how, in any event, the minister is going to check and collect this tax on stocks that are at present in hand. Under the other system he could collect on new goods that came in, but he is going to have a tremendous amount of difficulty in collecting this tax, and there is going to be a tremendous amount of leakage and losses. To do the thing properly you would require an audit of every retail establishment in Canada. Just to say that, indicates the difficulty of levying this tax on every item covered by this schedule. I think the minister ought to try to justify this tax on the basis of equity, and by that I mean the differentiation between small things. Why should cheap jewellery be exempted from the tax and candy be taxed? I say to the minister, if this is a proper tax, tax everything. I think I understand what his answer will be, that on small articles the cost of collection would be greater than the revenue that came in. Is not that the answer?
Mr. ILSLEY; Yes.	.

It would cost a good deal more than you would get out of it. That is the answer. This tax is in favour of Mr. Woolworth or Mr. Zeller, who deal in cheap kinds of merchandise. They will not be subject to this tax, but a reputable jewellery firm will have its business killed-people who are substantial business men in the community. I go along my own main street in Fredericton and see two old-established jewellers. One of them runs the finest store in town. I go up to the next block, and I see the cheap, tawdry jewellery that is found in the 5-and-10-cent store. The one who is taxed under this resolution is going to be put out of business, while the other fellow rakes in the shekels by the thousands and thousands on a multitude of small sales. I do not like this tax; I do not think it is fair. I do not see how in the world you are going to administer this tax on a proper basis. You cannot check it; you cannot control it. The only place to levy it is at the manufacturer's level, by adding the tax to the invoice. That is the way to do this thing: add it to the manufacturer's price. Then you will require returns only from a limited number of business people who will make correct returns. You will be saved the huge cost of auditing
Special War Revenue Act

and of collection, and you will get an honest return from the manufacturer. He is not going to take any chance; the tax is added to his bill, and he collects it as part of his invoice. The consumer always pays. You can take it as axiomatic that the consumer has to pay these taxes. There is the odd case where the "squeeze", if I may use that term, is applied as between wholesaler and retailer; sometimes they are made to absorb part of the tax, but in nine cases out of ten the consumer pays these bills.
You are trying to do something which I think will be very difficult of accomplishment, especially under to-day's conditions. Where the goods are already in the hands of the retailer there will be endless trouble. If you collect from one you must collect from all, and if you do this properly the cost of collection is going to be colossal; you will need a whole army of tax auditors, and we have enough now. I suggest to the minister that the proper principle is the one he is applying to candy.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This tax since it was announced has given me more trouble than any of the others.
I thought it would be a headache.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For various reasons. I think that would be a fair description of it-a headache; and I am going to propose a change in the resolution. But I want to tell the committee in my own language the reason why I did not think we should impose the tax at the manufacturer's level. Once it was decided to impose a tax of this weight, which is heavy-25 per cent-at the retailer's level, it became apparent that to impose a tax of this weight at the manufacturer's level would mean that the tax on jewellery would probably be 66 per cent or something like that, because of the great mark-up there is on jewellery; and even if a tax of 50 per cent at the manufacturer's level were imposed, many of the consequences would be extremely serious.
To whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
To various persons interested. I will give the committee some of the consequences of doing that. In the first place, if there were any difference in the degree to which retailers had stocked up there would be a tremendous amount of injustice. For instance, let us say the leader of the opposition is a retailer and has a small stock, and I am a retailer-perhaps running a department store- in a big way, and have very carefully stocked up and have a heavy inventory, and a tax goes on at 50 per cent of the manufacturer's

level. The leader of the opposition finds himself in an awkward position, finding himself carrying on business in competition with me, because he has to buy in at this high tax these goods which are very highly taxed, whereas my store is full of goods which are not taxed at all. The most serious discriminations would arise as between retailers, assuming there is a difference in the degree to which they have stocked inventories-and we are told that is the situation in the country at the present time. They are not evenly stocked in respect of inventories.
Well, they never are, are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: With a high manufacturer's tax that would create serious discrimination and injustice as between retailers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, but in a very much
smaller degree. In jewellery, I think it would be something like 66 per cent. That is one objection. Another objection to imposing the tax at the manufacturer's level' is that all the inventories would escape the tax. We do not know how great the inventories in Canada in the hands of retailers are at the present time. The hon. member for Lethbridge took me severely to task the other day for not knowing. He said we certainly should know what the inventories were and where they were. I wish I did, but I do not. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. Some of them are
slow moving and some of them are faster moving. That is the reason why we have separated this tax into two classes.

explain the difference between increased inventories and consumer hoarding,?

speechtext:

and I think the answer to that query is not as obvious as it is in the mind of the-hon. gentleman.

I think

I wish to ask him a question with respect to item 5-"articles of china, porcelain, earthenware. stoneware or other pottery ware, except articles for use in the preparation or serving of food or drink." Would that cover table china?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is exempted.

What is contemplated other than that?
Mr. ILSLEY; Porcelain ornaments, vase3,
ct cetera.

Ornamental
articles?
Mr. ILSLEY; Yes.
Not articles of general utility.
