speechtext: That is right.

A few days ago a merchant advertised a sale of handbags at $1.79 each. A buyer went in and bought one of

these and handed the merchant a five dollar bill, and when the change was given it was discovered that the merchant had charged more than SI.79. Asked why, he said the government had imposed a tax of 50 cents. In other words, he charged $1.79 plus 50 cents, but the purchaser received no slip with stamps on it. The purchaser did receive a slip with the total amount, but it bore no stamps. In what way will the government keep track of such sales? In most of the states to the south there is a turn-over tax, the equivalent of 3 per cent, from which they receive a large revenue. The state of Illinois receives about $50,000,000 a year. I am not advocating that, because I do not know enough about what a turn-over tax would mean here. Has the minister considered anything of that kind different from what I have quoted about the purchaser of this handbag, for which 50 cents extra was charged, and on the sales slip for which there where no stamps from which the government could receive anything?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The tax should have been 45 cents, not 50 cents.
I figured it at 44 cents, but the purchaser paid 50 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ever since the budget came down there has been some confusion in the minds of retailers as to just what they should do. The instructions were that they should place a stamp on the bill, cancel that stamp, and present to the purchaser the bill with the stamp so cancelled.
That was not done in this instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In some instances it has not been done, and there has been some lack of uniformity in practice. Once this resolution passes, it will make clear what the practice is, and it is hoped that there will be uniformity in the future.

Has the department made any investigation as to stocks carried prior to the introduction of this resolution, by such companies as, for instance, Eatons and Simpsons, as compared with the stocks they carried at the time of the last budget a year ago?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
I am informed by some merchants that they cannot meet the prices owing to the fact that, as they believed, certain stocks were materially increased just prior to the coming into force of the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
So far as the tax at the retail level is concerned, it attaches to stocks sold to the public. That is the best reason

Special War Revenue Act
in the world for fixing a retail tax. I would have stuck to it had it not been for the great administration difficulties and other reasons all along the line, but it is going to be more easily administered on jewellery than on some other lines which we have moved back to the manufacturer's level.

With regard to the item as it appears in the resolution before us, "clock and watches"-I suppose that should be "clocks"-will alarm clocks be exempt? I ask that because they are a necessity to certain workers. The same applies to military watches presented to soldiers. Sometimes these watches have the names engraved on them. Are such watches exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Alarm clocks are certainly a necessity to munitions workers. Clock manufacturers are to-day regulated almost out of business because priorities have practically put a stop to their producing clocks and watches. They are almost out of business because they cannot get the necessary materials, and I think they should have some leeway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If that is the situation, that is the best reason that can be given, so that people will not buy them who do not need them. That is one purpose of the tax. Not all clocks and watches are by any means necessities.
That is why I mentioned alarm clocks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At present the great majority of them are bought by persons who could get along without them. That is not so in every instance, but I do not think we can go round picking out those cases that should be exempt. I do not believe we can draw definitions or make rules that will be as accurate as that.
What kind of help are you going to give the manufacturer if he is put out of business by this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This will not put the manufacturer out of business. He will use what materials are available, make what he can with them and sell them all. The jewellers will sell everything they have; there is no doubt about that. This tax will slow up the sales to some extent I hope, put a little brake on the free purchasing of goods like this.
Of course that is the intention of the tax, to prevent the consumer from buying.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, that is one intention.

I wish the minister would apply that all along the line. There are other things we can get along without better than some of these things; whisky is one, but I am not going to revert to that.
I notice in the amendment there is a proviso at the end:
Provided that in the case of items mentioned under subparagraph 1 . . .
That refers to trunks, I think?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Trunks; suitcases; baggage and luggage of all kinds . . . the said tax shall not apply when they are manufactured expressly for a customer for his use in the operation of his business or profession.
That was not in the previous resolution, was it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
What is the reason for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Repair bags for telephone men is an example. Some firms make lines which constitute quite a large percentage of their total output, which are required-
Commercial travellers' luggage, for instance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, if it is used for business purposes it is a business expense; it is not the idea to tax that kind of thing.
And doctor's bags and lawyers' brief-cases, they will be exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
What about the luggage of a member of parliament when he has to travel all the time? I wish the minister could see some of mine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I do not know; I cannot give too many rulings.

I wish to call attention to a principle in this resolution which I think is very unfair. I admit it is not new; it is found in many other statutes. I think it is important, particularly since this item is under the general heading "Special War Revenue Act." I think it is a fair principle to appeal to this committee on, that is to say, that war taxes should rest as equally as possible on every Canadian citizen. This tax is on the retailer's price. If it is an imported article, the 25 per cent ad valorem tax is added to the price including the duty and other taxes. It will be seen that persons who reside in the more remote sections of Canada are

Special War Revenue Act

at a disadvantage as compared with those who live in the two central provinces where practically all these items are manufactured. In my province of Saskatchewan I do not believe there is a single item mentioned in the schedule of this resolution that does not have to be brought in from Ontario or Quebec or possibly British Columbia. The result is that the purchaser or consumer in Saskatchewan-I say Saskatchewan merely to give point to my submission-has to pay the 25 per cent on the price f.o.b. factory, plus freight, plus the mark-up, and that mark-up of course is made on the laid-down price in the merchant's store in Saskatchewan, with the result that the consumer pays considerably more because of the application of the percentage tax than do consumers in other parts of Canada more favourably situated. Or, if the article is imported, the same result follows; the consumer in Saskatchewan must pay the tax on the price including duty and taxes.
There are dozens of statutes in which that particular unfairness falls upon persons living in provinces other than Ontario and Quebec. It is often argued in this committee, I think without any attempt at contradiction, that the people of my province are peculiarly unable to bear that added tax. Yet this section imposes an added burden on those people simply because they live in a remote part of Canada where manufacturing industries are not located.
I would like the minister to consider estimating what the 25 per cent would amount to in cents or dollars and make the tax applicable in that manner rather than as a percentage.
I would hope also that the minister would keep in mind the principle that the people who reside in the more remote parts of Canada are continually irritated by the application of the pyramiding system and having the tax imposed on the pyramided price. I think the minister should carefully consider this matter, in order that the people may feel that war taxes are being imposed on every citizen as equitably as possible.

I should like to support the argument of the hon. member for Swift Current. There are many of these taxes that bear heavily on people resident in provinces like Saskatchewan. A year or two ago a tax was imposed on electric power. Our small local communities with their little power plants pay a terrific tax, while in this city, for example, where power is very cheap, the tax amounts to scarcely anything. Wherever the price is high, there you have the high tax.
I think the hon. member's representation is valid. There was a time when we used to see goods advertised at so much more west of the 
great lakes, on account, we were told, of freight. It is true that the freight is a little higher, and other things are higher. As the hon. member says, our people are not feeling any benefit from war activity; we have no war industries in the province, and this form of taxation does bear very heavily upon regions such as he mentioned.
I can see the difficulty of adopting some other method, but I believe it could be worked out so as to be much more equitable. Our people on the prairies are feeling, and have felt for the past two or three years, that while there has been a certain measure of, shall I say, war prosperity in some parts of the dominion, the taxation increase to a very large degree bears more heavily upon them and they find it hard to bear.,

In support of the remarks of the hon. member for Swift Current and the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar I should like to call to the attention of the Minister of Finance that we in the province of Quebec already have a 4 per cent sales tax which increases considerably the cost of these various articles. Besides that, we have the heavy taxation of our public utilities. I hold no brief for the power companies in the province of Quebec, but I believe something like $10,000,000 to $12,000,000 in taxes on these corporations is paid to the federal government, and that is shouldered by the consumer. So if the minister could see his way clear to heed the remarks of those hon. members, he might also have consideration for the situation of those in Quebec province.

I wish to support what was said by the hon. member for Peterborough West with regard to clocks. As a matter of fact, when the hon. member spoke I was about to rise to deal with the same subject. Most of the people in my constituency are interested in alarm clocks, and I want to draw the attention of the minister to the fact that an alarm clock is not a thing of beauty; no one would ever purchase one for its appearance. It sounds even worse than it looks, particularly about half past four o'clock in the morning.
Or even five o'clock.

Yes, or even five o'clock.
I have no doubt the hon. member for Davenport has heard it on occasion, and it is not a nice sound, especially on a nasty morning. As I have said, no one would buy an alarm clock if he did not have to, and instead of having to pay a tax on it I think he should be given an alarm clock as a bonus, whenever he has need of one. For these reasons I think, as a special concession to those who

Special War Revenue Act
have to do the sweating-I mean the physical sweating-in producing the sinews of war, if the minister cannot see his way clear to have alarm clocks given as bonuses, at least he should have them exempted from this tax.

I am curious as to why a 25 per cent tax was arrived at in connection with each group of articles. As I examine groups 1, 2, 3 and so on, I find very little relationship between them. For instance, there is not much connection between the commodities contained in group 2 and those contained in group 3, while the articles listed in group 2 are probably more essential than those listed in group 6. I rather feel that unless there is some strong justification for setting what I regard as a flat 25 per cent rate, there should be some variation, taking into consideration the part played in the lives of the people of this country by the various commodities.

I should like the minister to express an opinion, if he would be kind enough, as to why the tax could not be expressed in cents or dollars, striking a reasonable average as between retail prices throughout Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If this were converted from an ad valorem to a specific tax, it would be impossible to say what number of cents or dollars a given article should pay. For instance, articles of jewellery range in price from a few cents to many thousands of dollars. One could not put a specific tax on jewellery of, say $1 per article.

No, but you could make it a specific tax, so many cents on jewellery up to a certain value; so many dollars on jewellery up to a certain higher value, and so on, grading the tax. I know that is a cumbersome method, but I suggest that it would be better to have this taxation principle correct and equitable, in order to remove the dissatisfaction that exists as between the different provinces, even though it meant going to a little more trouble in interpreting the tax. I think it will be agreed that our taxation system has spread out so enormously that the department must be prepared to face a certain amount of trouble and difficulty in the interpretation and application of these taxes.
I wonder if the minister would care to satisfy me, if that is possible, with respect to the setting of the 25 per cent tax in each case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, we had a list of articles most of which people could do without, if they wanted to. We cut out a great many
44561-263J
categories, after consideration, and these were left. The great bulk of these are articles the purchase of which, generally speaking, can be deferred. That is true of a great many of them, if not all. There is no scientific method of ascertaining the correct rate. Twentynfive per cent for each is just as likely to be correct as 25 per cent for some, 20 per cent for others and 15 per cent for others. It is just as appropriate as the 8 per cent sales tax over the whole range of goods, for example, and perhaps more so.
If I understood the minister correctly a moment ago, he said that brief-cases of lawyers would be exempt from this tax.
The clients will pay the-tax.	*

What did the minister
say when the leader of the opposition asked whether brief-cases of lawyers were exempted?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is an amendment
which exempts articles included in the first item when used in business, or something of the kind; I do not know the exact words. It is a question of interpretation as to what that covers.

That was what I had in mind. In that connection I wanted to ask if brief-cases or sample cases of commercial travellers, architects, engineers and a long list of people who have to use these articles in earning their living also will be exempt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am told that brief-cases
and catalogue cases were crossed out entirely.
They are exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, brief-cases and catalogue cases are crossed out.
And engineers' cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know, I am sure.
Do not involve me in too difficult questions of interpretation.
Brief-cases of architects,, and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would need to have the
item before me.

I support the principle that the tax should be collected at the point of sale, for many reasons which I do not think it necessary to point out. In group 6, however, I should like to point out that articles of china are included. There is very little china manufactured in Canada. The great percentage of the china sold in our stores is manufactured in Great Britain, and a very large part of it is reexported to the United
Special War Revenue Act

States. We who live along the border between the United States and Canada do quite a business in selling china to citizens of the United States who come here for that express purpose, that is tourists who come to Canada quite often for that one purpose. They make a special trip for it, and we sell them china which is manufactured in Great Britain. That serves two>
purposes, and I think we should allow that china to go out of this country without paying this extra charge. In selling it we help the British people, who make it, and we obtain United States dollars. My suggestion to the minister is that for export purposes the tax on china should be dispensed with.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think it would be pretty
hard to determine whether or not a buyer was really a tourist. That is the trouble with making tourist exemptions. We gave some consideration to that, but we felt that it would be administratively difficult. It will be noted that china for use in the preparation or serving of food or drink is not covered by the item; it is only articles of china which are ornamental in character that are dealt with. I know tourists buy some of those, but I am afraid they will have to pay the tax like anybody else.

The minister has announced that the tax on some of these articles is to be collected at the source, and in his remarks he said that there were large stocks of these articles in the hands of some of the large retailers. How is the tax going to be collected on the articles now in the retail stores? Will they be exempt?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

There has been a number
of these articles sold and the 25 per cent tax has been collected. What is to happen about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We shall have to validate
that tax so that there will not be refunds.
Can the minister tell whether the delegation which recently waited upon him represented the larger or the smaller retail stores?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A number of delegations
have waited upon me, and I think all interests and all points of view have been represented. I think the smaller retailers have been adequately represented by the retail merchants' association of Canada. Mr. Hougham, whom I have known for some years, represents that association. Representations have been made by the small retailers, the large retailers, the wholesalers, the manufacturers and everybody but the consumers. (Mr. Tripp.]

As a retailer I cannot follow
the argument of the minister in regard to stocks on hand, nor can I see how it will be fair to the smaller retailer. The minister has said that there is no check up with regard to stocks on hand. If I am not greatly mistaken, he will find this information in the bureau of statistics. A merchant must fill out a form giving information to June 30, not only what he has at the end of June but his purchases separately for the months of January, February, March, April, May and June, and then his total sales as well. It should be possible to make a very close estimate of the stocks on hand as of June 30. I do not think the minister has looked into this matter as fully as he generally does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My advisers tell me that
they could not obtain accurate information, but I am interested in what my hon. friend says.

I think
they must have slipped.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know. It may be
that moving some of these articles back to the manufacturer's level will not work very well for certain retailers, but it must be borne in mind that articles of a greater value are remaining at the retailer's level.

I do not know that I have
a great deal of objection to your moving them back, but now that you have started it I think it would have been better to have left the seven or eight items as they were originally.

The objection to that would be the cost of administration, and there -would be all kinds of chiseling. There would be a great loss of revenue, great expense in administration and the taxes would be wiped out. My reaction to this resolution was that the simplest method would be to work on the manufacturer's cost. No doubt the minister and his advisers, subject to the one omission that the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) has indicated, have studied this question more than anyone else has found it possible to do. Perhaps the minister is justified in what he has said. However, having regard to the information I have and the growing scarcity of consumer goods, I think that if large purchases have been made by the larger retailers it must be known to the bureau of statistics. I make the prediction that within twelve months the shelves of the small retailers in this country will be bare; many of them are bare now. If you were in England you would be astonished at the lack of commodities in the

Special War Revenue Act
small shops, but if you went to Harrod's or Selfridge's or any of the other large stores you would find that they were just full' of merchandise. I predict that within twelve months Eatons, Simpsons and the other large stores will have huge stocks of consumer goods on hand, while the shelves of the small retailer will be bare.
They say they are increasing their warehouses now.

That may be just gossip. I am going to ask the minister .to get in touch with his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), and ask him to reveal between now and three o'clock to-morrow afternoon the information available in his department with respect to the stocks of these commodities on hand. The senior hon. member for Halifax has indicated that this information should be available. The large stores are well stocked up, and there is going to be a tremendous discriminatory effect upon the small retailers of this country. They are going to be a war casualty; in fact, many of them are now. In addition, they have to pay higher income taxes.
The big man has the inside track.

If I said that, the minister would say that I was speaking politically, but perhaps the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) can say that to the minister. I do not like to throw out that kind of insinuation unless I have proof. If I had the proof I would say it; do not make any mistake about that. The large stores have an advantage because of their great buying power, and in addition to that they have better business acumen. They are able to look into the future with better results, and that is why they have grown.

Has the minister any recent information as to whether the number of retail stores is increasing or decreasing? I have noticed lately when walking along the streets of Toronto that there are more stores vacant, which would indicate that many small merchants are going out of business. The smaller merchants upon whom I have called recently all tell me that they are going to be put out of business by the taxes being imposed upon them, and the number of vacant stores would indicate that something serious is happening. I do not know whether this budget will increase or decrease the amount of revenue when so many merchants are being forced out of business. It would depend on
whether the number of retailers is increasing or decreasing. Has the minister any information on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I have not, but I know that in 1941 the volume of goods sold by retail stores was 25 per cent greater than before the war, and the dollar value was about 50 per cent greater. There was a tremendous increase in business.
Because thei;e was a great deal more buying power.
My question was whether the number of retail stores was increasing or decreasing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information on that.

I had no intention of criticizing the minister in my remarks about the big man having the inside track. What I meant to convey to the leader of the opposition and to the house was that men in the wartime prices and trade board who are connected with large concerns are in a position to know the exact situation about shortages and to advise their firms accordingly. I do not say that they are doing it, but they are in a position to do it, many of them being connected with large firms. But I had no intention of criticizing the minister for that.

Then I misinterpreted the hon. gentleman. There is something in what he says. I have observed over a period of years the trend against the small retailer in our communities throughout Canada because of the chain store. It is a grave problem. The small retailer gives credit; the chain stores do not. The small retailer is a part of the community and takes part in the community life. But who ever heard of a chain store taking part in community life? I can remember that when I went to Fredericton forty years ago, we had five or six first-class grocery stores, big concerns which carried everything and did a huge business. The proprietors of these stores were among our leading citizens. They took part in every phase of our community life, and I have no doubt that the minister knows of a similar situation in his home town. To-day there is not one such big grocery store in Fredericton. They have all been driven out by the chain store. That is a factor in the life of our communities of which we must take note. I am just a bit fearful of this trend. I do not know just how you are going to curb it. I do know that by means of taxation and that sort of thing, attempts have been made on many occasions to curb this trend; but after all, before the war at all
Special War Revenue Act

events, we were living in a land of free enterprise. The people do not have to support these chain stores, but they do, and I am just a little afraid that this taxation will accentuate the situation.

I wish to return to the point I raised a few moments ago because I believe there is a very important principle of taxation involved. May I ask the minister if he recognizes the inequality that results from this type of tax imposition because of the pyramiding process in the application of a tax on a percentage basis?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On some goods on which the cost of transportation is added to the manufacturer's price the consumer at a distance will undoubtedly pay more per article than a consumer in other parts of Canada who buys nearer to the point of production. But there are articles on which the price is equalized all over the country.
Not so many.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps not many, but there are some, and to those that objection would not apply. I would' point out that while that objection may apply to most of the articles in this list, our sales tax, which is by far the largest tax on the sale of goods, escapes very largely that objection because it is imposed at the manufacturer's level and does not include transportation. With respect to the electricity tax, which is small, and this tax, which is small-the total amount to be derived from this tax in a full year is only $7,750,000-it may be that a case, not a very large case, I think, can be made out, but I do not think it is a very large grievance. On grounds, of strict fairness, however, as between consumers in different parts of Canada it may be said that a consumer at a place remote from the point of production will pay a little more per article. But that cannot be avoided if we are going to impose the tax at the retailer's level. On the bulk of these articles it must go on at the retailer's level. Otherwise the heavy inventories will escape and discriminations between persons with large inventories and persons with small inventories will arise. There would be an undesirable stimulation to consumer spending if we imposed a very high tax at the manufacturer's level, leaving the inventories in the retail stores untaxed.

I raised the point, not
Because of the items covered by this resolution but because of the principles which, as the minister points out, are applicable to all measures of taxation. The application of my objection goes further even than the addition

of the freight rate to the price at the point of manufacture, because there are certain trade practices such as mark-up. On jewellery, for instance, I assume that the trade mark-up by the retailer is likely 100 per cent. There is also a veiy high mark-up on furniture and many other articles which represents a very considerable percentage of the laid-down price in the store. This tax and other taxes of a like nature on the retail price are applied not only on the base price at point of manufacture but on that price plus freight and mark-up, and the application of the tax on that pyramided price is very unfair. I trust that the minister is quite aware of that inequity and that if he has a reasonable opportunity of removing it he will do so.

What position will the western provinces be in as compared with the central provinces under this tax. It is well known that the central provinces are the manufacturers of almost all the things we buy in western Canada, and western Canada, the orphan of Canada at the present time, will be compelled to pay a higher price than the central provinces for the articles we are now discussing.
Am I right in understanding the minister to say that present stocks were exempt from this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. The present stocks of most of these articles are taxable, and with respect to some I am proposing an amendment to move the tax back to the manufacturer's level, so that hereafter, after to-night, stocks of these articles in retail stores will be free from tax.

I think the hon. member for Assiniboia was anxious to have a clear understanding in regard to the large stocks of these articles now held by the larger retail stores. My understanding was the same as that of the hon. member, that what they now have on hand would not be taxed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

I think the leader of the opposition has raised a very important point. I do not wish to take any strong stand against large stores, but it would appear to me that the smaller stores are labouring under a handicap in this respect.
They certainly are.

It is a well-known and recognized fact that during the past two years, and particularly last year, the large stores have had buyers in the field buying wherever it was possible.

Special War Revenue Act
Trying to get whole outfits.

It will be shown, I believe, in the report which has been asked for that their stocks have increased to a marked extent. I might add, for the benefit of the minister, that if I remember rightly, the date on which this return is to be made is July 18. I do not see how it is possible to have the return compiled and sent in by that date. I wish to add my voice to that of the leader of the opposition in urging the minister to give this matter serious thought.
While the chairman may rule that what I am about to say has no direct bearing upon the resolution under discussion, I am going to point out something else. Smaller retailers throughout Canada, and particularly on the eastern coast, feel that discrimination is being shown in favour of the larger stores in the manner in which the parking and non-parlcing regulations are being put into effect. The large stores have the advantage of extensive parking spaces, while the smaller stores do not enjoy that benefit. It has been said-I do not say it-that this is due to the dollar-a-year men being in a position to affect directly traffic and other matters which work to the real benefit of the large stores. While this may have no direct bearing on the resolution under discussion, it may be one more little indication pointing to favouritism in so far as the large stores are concerned.

So far as I am concerned I want to facilitate the passage of the minister's resolution. But I would ask him, in view of the discussion which was raised here this evening, not to press this item but to go on to another one and, between now and to-morrow, when we meet again, have his officials get all the information available with respect to stocks in the big department stores-
And the warehouses.

-and in warehouses, at a certain stated period. I think this will be interesting and useful information.
I am not going to throw out any insinuations, but it is true that Mr. Burton's son is in charge of retail sales in the wartime prices and trade board. I think it would be better if he were not there. No doubt he is one of the best retail men in Canada, but do you not see where it gives an opportunity to question a man's integrity when he puts himself in that position. He is there as a dollar-a-year man; he knows what is going on; he is paid by his firm-one of the biggest retailers in the country. I am not making any attack on him at
all, but there is the opportunity for a misunderstanding, and it seems to me that men ought not to allow themselves to be put in that position. No wonder there is criticism when an appointment like that is made, having regard to the ramifications of his own employment and the knowledge which he gets as a result of his dollar-a-year position. I just throw that out as a suggestion to the minister. I am not making any charge. No doubt he is one of the most conscientious men in the world. But these men leave themselves liable to charges by people who perhaps are not fair about it.
I ask the minister to get the information the committee asks for with respect to the stocks of the big retailers. If what the senior hon. member for Halifax says is correct, the minister can get it from the bureau of statistics.
While I am on my feet might I make this suggestion to the minister. Last year the sets of resolutions were not reported one by one as they were passed, but he reserved the time of the report until several sets were passed, and then introduced the bills. If he would have each set of resolutions reported to the Chair as they are passed and a bill introduced, we would have more time to study the bill. I think it would be fair to hon. members to do that. For instance, this afternoon we passed one set of resolutions dealing with the Excise Act. I would ask if, before we rise to-night, the minister would have these resolutions reported and then introduce the bill, so that we may get the bill and study it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will get the bills in as fast as I can arrange it, but the legal work of preparation of these bills and the work of checking is tremendous, and I do not know that the bill on the Excise Act will be ready to-night.

What I am thinking about is the introduction of the bill so that we may see it and study it. We are near the end of this session, and things will be done in a hurry. All the time you can give us to study the bill is important to us. The minister and his officials know what they are doing, but we do not know it until we see the printed bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will bear that in mind and get the bills in just as fast after the resolutions are passed as is possible.
It is all right for this item to stand, but I must make it clear that the arrangements under the resolution will have to be as stated in the amendment. That is a peculiarity of our system; there must not be any
Special War Revenue Act

vacuum; there must not be any interim period. The taxes on certain of these items go off to-night as of to-morrow morning; either they do or they do not, and there cannot be any doubt about it, because otherwise there will be speculation on what eventually will be done. So it must be taken, I think, that the amendment I proposed is settled as far as trading to-morrow is concerned.
Well, that is notice to the public, anyway.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is notice to the public. I want to make that clear. May I say that no one has a keener appreciation than I myself of the difficulties in this matter as indicated in the observations of the hon. senior member for Halifax. I never know in these things whether somebody has been benefited a little at the expense of somebody else, or not, but I heard all the representations, and when the retail association of Canada, with Mr. George Hougham representing them, a man who is always associated in my mind with the representation of the smaller rather than the larger retailers, although I think he represents all, was in favour of moving all these articles back to the manufacturer's level, while I decided not to do that on the bulk of them for the very reasons that the hon. senior member for Halifax advanced to-night, I did think I should do it on items yielding about two million dollars of revenue here, because of the difficulties of administration that have developed since I introduced the budget, the tales of woe that we have had-
The end is not yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
-about employing new
staffs. I do not want to say anything about my friend the commissioner of excise, but he has a responsibility about these matters, and he does not like to assume the responsibility of enforcing a tax unless it is enforced.
Of course, his duties are administrative. They are not legislative.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but as an administrator he has every right to make representations to the Minister of Finance and say, "Now, if you give me that thing to enforce, I am afraid that I can't enforce it."

Does the
minister ever heed that advice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Time after time. Sometimes I do not, but usually I do. I do if I can, because I know what his difficulties are.

I was minister of that department for five years, and I have repeatedly said in this chamber that this house should take great care to see, when it enacts laws, that it enacts the kind of laws which the people will respect and which can be enforced reasonably well. In some respects, I am afraid, this is a little . off the line, but we have kept it on to the extent that we felt we could, and the recommendations I have made to-night embody the result of my judgment and that of my officials, after a very considerable amount of discussion and a great many difficulties. I am content to let that rest until to-morrow. With regard to what was said about the administrators, I do not object at all to any remarks like that.
I realize that when we go out and select executives of department stores and put them in the position of administrators of the retail trade or anything else, it will be said that they are using their positions, to help themselves and the interests with which they have been connected.

I did not
say that, I said that they were open to the charge that they might, I did not suggest that they did. I was very guarded in what I said. But they are open to that charge by virtue of their taking those positions and still retaining their connections with their parent firms. By so doing they lay themselves open to the chaige.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What are we to do about it? Consider the position the government is in.
If we do not take men who know the business, we must take someone who does not know the business and who will have no authority in administering it. That is the difficulty. We try to get round that by taking particularly able civil servants where we find them, and when we do that we are bitterly criticized for taking theorists-
Impractical men.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -and brain trusters.
Men without practical experience.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. Sometimes we get bankers. We have asked the banks to release some of their best men, and they do. We have put these men in responsible positions. Often they are very good; they are excellent. They have practical business experience and financial experience as well; their heads are level, and so on. But how often have I heard it said that they are favouring their old clients. How often have I heard that statement made? I have heard it in this house. Members in this house say that there should be occupational representation on the war-

Special War Revenue Act
time prices and trade board. That statement has been made repeatedly, and I have risen and said1, "no occupational representation on the board. A dozen civil servants; that is all we will have". Then it is objected that we are relying on men without practical experience. But if we once started putting on, that board representatives of particular callings or occupations, making it a kind of parliament where each had' a constituency to represent instead of representing the interests of the dominion as a whole, as civil servants are very likely to do-and in practically every case they do-I am sure we would be in a great deal more trouble than we are in at the present time. Whatever course we take is open to certain objections. Generally speaking, the course that has been followed with the wartime prices and trade board has been to look for ability which has been developed as a result of experience, together with character, and then to disregard the charges that these men are advancing their own interests. If anyone knows wherein they have done so, let him tell me or let him say it in the house.

We have heard it.
Mr. 1LSLEY: Certainly no one wants anything of that kind to go on.
How many more employees will be required across the country, from coast to coast, to carry out the provisions of all these extra taxes? Several people have asked that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just under this resolution?

Under all
of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say. The hon. gentleman is not referring to the income tax?
No; the number of employees that will be involved as a result of the new budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would be impossible to say. It will be a great many, but I have no means of estimating the number.
Resolution stands.
16.	That immediately after the word "cameras" in section five of schedule I to the said act, be added the following words:.
"photographic films and plates; projectors for slides, films or pictures; except those designed exclusively for industrial or professional photographers'use	25 per cent."
What effect will this have on the motion-picture industry. Will they have to pay?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. Is the hon. member referring to such concerns as the Associated Screen News, for example? Those would be films, projectors, and so on for industrial or professional photographers' use.

They
come under the exception?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
This is ordinaiy photographic material?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

As one of thousands of amateur photographers in Canada I know I am correct when I say that the present retail prices of photographic films, plates and projectors are so high now that very few people can afford to buy them or to use them; but if you jump the price 25 per cent, why except those designed exclusively for industrial or professional photographers' use? Take the film designed for the amateur's use; it is, in most instances, identical with that designed for professional use. Therefore, if you are going to increase the price of films 25 per cent to the amateur, you should do so in the case of the industrial or professional user. By not including the industrial or professional user you overlook a great source of income, because much more film and many more projectors are used by them, and they make a profit on the purchase, resale and use of the film and projector, whereas the amateur makes nothing. Why not tax the profit?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was not designed in order to impose an additional business tax. This is a consumer's tax. To put it on business would increase the cost of carrying on business at a time when price ceilings prevent increases in charges and when heavy income taxes and business and excess profits taxes take excess earnings. In short, this was not designed as a business tax or as an additional cost in doing business.

In this legislation the minister is getting around the price ceiling. He is putting the price up 25 per cent when it is high enough now, and, as I say, the professional photographer uses films designed exactly as those used by the amateur. How will you tell them apart? What makes a man a professional? Suppose I make a film to-day and sell it; I go into the professional class. Shall I get my films the next day at 25 per cent less than I get them to-day when I am an amateur? It is not fair.

There are many schools throughout the country that have motion-picture projectors. The inspectors

Special War Revenue Act

take pictures and show them throughout their districts. Would the films that they buy be taxable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

That is going to hamper education to a great extent. These motion-picture cameras use kodachrome, and with the extra tax a film is going to cost practically $7 for fifty feet. Four hundred feet of film will show in about fifteen minutes; $7 for one-eighth of a roll will make the whole roll cost about $56 with the tax.

There is a determining
factor in this resolution, the person for whom the camera or film was designed. Reading the resolution strictly, who is going to determine what films are designed exclusively for industrial or professional photographers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They are of a distinguishable type, I am told. This applies not only to films but plates, projectors, et cetera. Any of those articles that are designed exclusively for the use of industrial or professional photographers are free of the tax; those that are not are taxable.
I suppose it is well understood in the trade.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think so.
17.	That section eight of said schedule I to the said act be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"9. Beverages consisting of unfermented fruit juices (not including grape and other native fruit juices where at least ninety-five per cent of the products sold consist of pure juice of the fruit) and imitations thereof, carbonated beverages or aerated waters and all other compounded or mixed soft _ drinks, put up in bottles for sale	 25 per cent and one cent per bottle."
Is the one cent a bottle for a pint or a quart bottle?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Any bottle.

Many speeches
were made this afternoon about endeavouring to cut down the sale of alcoholic beverages. It is rather a pity that this extra tax should go on soft drinks. I think if it were kept to a reasonable level they would probably take the place of alcoholic beverages to some extent.
Oh, oh.
I mean what I say; I think it is a pity. I think cutting down the cost of soft drinks would have some effect in reducing the consumption of alcoholic beverages.

I have
heard of people buying chocolates instead of alcohol, but I never heard of them buying coca-cola.

What was the clause
before it was changed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The part in italics is new
and the one cent per bottle is new.
What were the proceeds from the tax last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amount last year was
$6,247,000. The estimated revenue from the increase in rate for a full year is $5,000,000. The estimated revenue for the increase in rate for the remainder of the fiscal year is $3,750,000.

Item agreed to.
18.	That the said schedule I to the said act is further amended by adding at the end thereof as section ten and eleven the following:
"10. Chocolate, candy and confectionery which may be classed as candy or a substitute for
candy	 30 per cent."
"11. Chewing gum	 30 per cent."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have an amendment to
propose. This resolution imposes a new tax of 30 per cent on manufacturers of chocolate, candies, et cetera. The amendment I have to propose is in the form of a proviso, the effect of which is to substitute for the 30 per cent tax in the case of items packaged by the manufacturers to sell normally in the retail trade for five cents, ten cents and fifteen cents, a tax of one cent, two cents and three cents respectively. This proposal is made with a view to equalizing the tax as between manufacturers of these classes of fixed price items. I believe it will find favour with the trade generally.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health

speechtext: And especially the small retailers.

I was just coming to that; especially the retailer in the small corner store. As has been pointed out to the committee already to-night by many hon. members, the small retailer is having a hard time to exist even now, and with taxes such as these it will become even more difficult. Then there is the child himself. As hon. members know, many children
Special War Revenue Act

get only a cent, and they go to the store and buy a cent's worth of candy. You may say, why not give them 2 cents? Well, being Scotch and thrifty, while a cent is a small amount of money, nevertheless it is well to bring up our children on small amounts of money, and then they will appreciate the value of money more -when they get older. Also it may be suggested that certain candies which sell three or four for a cent could be sold at two for a cent instead. Well, if the retailer does that, the wartime prices and trade board will come along and say he is increasing the price of his candy, and he will not be permitted to do so. So the small merchant is met with difficulty at every turn, making it harder than ever for him to carry on. I would have hoped that some consideration might be given with regard to candies selling for less than 5 cents.

I have had a number of protests in my constituency, most of which I have sent on to the minister. They have come from the retailer, the storekeeper, who has given me figures somewhat similar to those mentioned by the hon. member for Brantford City. The storekeepers who have written me have assured me that if this tax remains, one-cent candy will go off the market. It is pretty well agreed and pretty well established, I think, by both the manufacturers and the retailers that if this tax stands, that class of candy goes out of existence. During the evening someone criticized a tax as a mean tax; in fact, I think two taxes were referred to in that way. But I do not know a meaner tax than that which takes candy from the babies.
I was not going to say that.

Someone ought to have said it. There are those who will say that the baby is better off without the candy, but I do not think that is a good argument. We are not the judges of that. I do think something should be done in this connection. We shall not hear from the children who are interfered with by this tax. The amount that will be raised is very small compared with the number of people who will be inconvenienced and who will feel aggrieved as a result of this legislation. I do think the minister should do something about what the leader of the opposition has described as the penny candy.
Progress reported.
Resolutions (Excise Act) reported, read the second time and concurred in.
